5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Supervise.use_when: Held-out evaluation: always, for every fine-tuning run, as a basic sanity check against overfitting. Human evaluation: for final validation before deploying a model to production, or when LLM-judge results are surprising/borderline and need ground truth. LLM-as-judge: for rapid iteration during development (comparing many fine-tuning configurations/checkpoints quickly) and for ongoing automated regression testing.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Supervise.avoid_when: Don't rely SOLELY on training/validation loss as your quality signal — low perplexity doesn't guarantee good responses (a model can have low loss while being repetitive, sycophantic, or subtly wrong in ways loss doesn't capture). Don't use LLM-as-judge as your ONLY evaluation for high-stakes decisions without periodic human-eval calibration — judge biases can silently mislead your optimization (e.g. optimizing for verbosity because the judge prefers longer answers).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Supervise.what_goes_wrong: Held-out set contamination — if the held-out set overlaps with training data (common with web-scraped datasets that have near-duplicates), 'good' held-out performance is illusory. LLM-as-judge biases: position bias (the judge favors whichever response is shown first/second depending on the model), length bias (favors longer responses regardless of quality), and self-preference bias (a model judge tends to prefer outputs in its own 'style', including outputs from itself or similar models) — all of which can systematically mislead which fine-tuning checkpoint looks 'best'.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Supervise.real_example: A typical SFT evaluation pipeline: track validation loss/perplexity during training to pick the best checkpoint (avoiding overfit checkpoints from later epochs), then run that checkpoint through an LLM-as-judge comparison against the previous production model on a curated set of representative prompts (using something like the 'MT-Bench' or 'AlpacaEval' methodology — pairwise comparison with position-swapping to reduce bias), and finally run a smaller human evaluation on a sample before full rollout — this three-tier approach balances speed (LLM-judge for fast iteration) with reliability (human eval as final gate).

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Why.what_it_is: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: a training pipeline that uses human preference judgments (which of two responses is better) to further train an LLM beyond SFT, so its outputs better match what humans actually want — helpful, honest, harmless responses — rather than just plausible-sounding text.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Why.why_it_exists: SFT teaches a model to imitate good demonstrations, but it can only be as good as the demonstrations — and for many qualities (helpfulness, tactfulness, avoiding subtle harms, calibrated confidence), it's much easier for humans to JUDGE which of two responses is better than to WRITE the ideal response from scratch. RLHF exploits this asymmetry: collect comparative preference data (cheaper/easier to gather at scale than perfect demonstrations) and use RL to optimize the model toward whatever the preference data implies is 'better'.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Why.how_it_works: Three stages: (1) Start from an SFT model. (2) Collect preference data — humans compare pairs of model outputs for the same prompt and indicate which is better; train a separate REWARD MODEL to predict this preference (outputs a scalar score for any (prompt, response)). (3) Use RL (typically PPO) to fine-tune the SFT model's policy to generate responses that the reward model scores highly, while a KL penalty keeps the policy from drifting too far from the SFT model (preventing reward hacking / degenerate outputs).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Why.use_when: Building a general-purpose assistant where 'quality' is multi-dimensional and hard to specify via demonstrations alone (helpfulness, harmlessness, tone, refusing appropriately) — this is the pipeline behind ChatGPT, Claude, and similar models' final alignment stage.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Why.avoid_when: RLHF is complex, expensive (requires training/maintaining a reward model AND running RL, with all its instability), and requires substantial human-labeling infrastructure — for narrower tasks, SFT alone or simpler preference-optimization methods (DPO) that skip the separate reward model and RL loop often get most of the benefit with far less complexity.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Why.what_goes_wrong: Reward hacking — the policy finds ways to score highly on the reward model WITHOUT actually being 'better' (e.g. excessive hedging, sycophancy, verbosity, because annotators/reward models tend to rate longer/more agreeable responses higher). RLHF can also induce a 'tax' on capabilities — models sometimes become measurably worse at certain tasks (e.g. creative writing diversity drops) after heavy RLHF, a known trade-off labs actively manage.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Why.real_example: InstructGPT (the predecessor to ChatGPT) demonstrated that a 1.3B RLHF model was preferred by human raters over the 175B GPT-3 base model on instruction-following — showing RLHF's outsized impact on PERCEIVED quality/alignment relative to raw scale, even though the RLHF model didn't 'know' more facts than the base model.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.what_it_is: The first stage of the RLHF pipeline: fine-tune the pretrained base model on a (usually modest-sized) dataset of human-written demonstrations — example (prompt, ideal response) pairs — to produce an initial instruction-following model that subsequent stages build on.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.why_it_exists: RLHF's later stages (reward modeling, PPO) need a reasonable STARTING POLICY — running RL from a raw base model (which doesn't reliably follow instructions or stay on-topic) would be extremely sample-inefficient and unstable, since the reward model would need to evaluate wildly varying, often nonsensical outputs. SFT gets the model into the 'right ballpark' of instruction-following behavior so RL can focus on REFINING quality rather than teaching the basic task format from scratch.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.how_it_works: Human labelers write high-quality responses to a diverse set of prompts (representative of expected production traffic — questions, instructions, creative tasks, etc.). The base model is fine-tuned on these (prompt, response) pairs with the standard supervised next-token objective (loss computed on response tokens). The resulting 'SFT model' serves two roles in later stages: it's the INITIAL POLICY for PPO, AND it's often used as the reference model for the KL penalty (keeping the RL-tuned policy from drifting too far from this starting point).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.use_when: Always the first step of any RLHF (or DPO) pipeline — you cannot skip directly to preference-based training from a raw pretrained model.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.avoid_when: N/A within an RLHF pipeline — but if your overall goal doesn't require RLHF (SFT alone meets your needs), you'd stop here and not proceed to reward modeling/PPO.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.what_goes_wrong: If the SFT demonstration set is too narrow (covers only a few prompt types), the resulting policy's behavior on OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION prompts during RLHF can be erratic, making reward model scoring and PPO training noisier. If SFT is run for too many epochs/too aggressively, the model can become 'overfit' to the demonstration style in ways that make it harder for PPO to subsequently improve (less exploration headroom).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.real_example: OpenAI's InstructGPT paper describes Step 1 as fine-tuning GPT-3 on ~13k prompts with labeler-written demonstrations — a relatively small but carefully curated dataset compared to GPT-3's original pretraining corpus, illustrating that this stage is about BEHAVIOR SHAPING, not knowledge injection.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.what_it_is: The second stage of RLHF: train a separate model (the 'reward model', RM) to take a (prompt, response) pair and output a scalar score predicting how much a human would prefer that response — trained on human-labeled comparisons between pairs of model outputs.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.why_it_exists: PPO (Step 3) needs a REWARD SIGNAL for every generated response to know whether to reinforce or discourage it — but you can't have a human in the loop scoring every single response during RL training (too slow/expensive, RL needs thousands-to-millions of samples). The reward model is a learned PROXY for human judgment that can be queried automatically and cheaply at RL training speed.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.how_it_works: Collect data: for a given prompt, generate multiple responses (often from the SFT model with different sampling), have human labelers RANK or pick the better of pairs. Train the RM (usually initialized from the SFT model, with the final layer replaced by a scalar output head) using a pairwise ranking loss — e.g. the Bradley-Terry model: loss = -log(sigmoid(r(prompt, chosen) - r(prompt, rejected))), which pushes the RM to assign a higher score to the human-preferred response than the rejected one, with the margin determined by how confidently labelers preferred it.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.use_when: Required for classic RLHF (PPO-based alignment) — if you're implementing the full RLHF pipeline as in InstructGPT/LLaMA-2-Chat. Also useful standalone as an evaluation tool (scoring/ranking candidate responses) even outside an RL loop.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.avoid_when: Preference-optimization methods like DPO skip this step entirely — they optimize the policy DIRECTLY on preference pairs using a loss derived to be mathematically equivalent (under certain assumptions) to RLHF's optimal policy, without needing a separate reward model or RL loop. If your goal is just 'align to preferences' without the operational complexity of maintaining/serving a reward model during training, DPO-family methods are simpler.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.what_goes_wrong: The reward model can have systematic BIASES that it then propagates into the policy during PPO — e.g. if labelers (even unconsciously) preferred longer or more confident-sounding responses, the RM learns to reward length/confidence regardless of actual quality, and PPO will exploit this ('reward hacking'). RM quality is capped by the quality and consistency of human labels — noisy/inconsistent preference data produces a noisy reward signal that misguides RL.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.real_example: InstructGPT's reward model was a 6B parameter model (smaller than the 175B policy) trained on ~33k prompts with K=4-9 ranked responses per prompt (converted into pairwise comparisons) — a relatively compact model whose ONLY job is to output a single number representing 'how good is this response', which then drives the much larger policy's training via PPO.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Rewa.what_it_is: The specific architectural and training details of the reward model: typically a transformer (often the SAME architecture/initialization as the policy/SFT model) with the language-modeling head replaced by a single linear layer that outputs ONE scalar value per (prompt, response) sequence, trained with a pairwise comparison loss.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Rewa.why_it_exists: Reusing the SFT model's architecture/weights as initialization gives the RM a head start — it already 'understands' language and the task domain, so it only needs to learn the additional mapping from (understanding) to (a scalar preference score), which requires far less data than learning language understanding from scratch.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Rewa.how_it_works: Take the transformer backbone (often initialized from the SFT checkpoint), remove the LM head (which outputs a distribution over vocabulary at each position), and add a small linear layer that maps the final hidden state (typically at the last token / end-of-sequence position) to a single scalar. Train with the Bradley-Terry pairwise loss on (prompt, chosen_response, rejected_response) triples: maximize the score gap between chosen and rejected. The RM is typically trained for just 1 epoch on preference data to avoid overfitting (RMs can quickly memorize the relatively small preference dataset, becoming poorly calibrated on the much larger distribution of responses PPO will generate).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Rewa.use_when: Whenever implementing the classic RLHF pipeline — RM architecture choices (model size relative to policy, initialization, training epochs) are important hyperparameters that significantly affect downstream PPO stability and final quality.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Rewa.avoid_when: If using DPO/IPO/KTO-style methods, there's no separate reward model to architect/train — these methods derive an IMPLICIT reward directly from the policy's and reference model's log-probabilities, sidestepping this entire component.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Rewa.what_goes_wrong: Reward model OVERFITTING — if trained too long on a limited preference dataset, the RM becomes very confident/sharp on in-distribution examples but poorly calibrated on the novel responses PPO generates as it explores — this miscalibration is a primary driver of reward hacking (PPO finds responses that are far outside the RM's training distribution but happen to score artificially high). Size mismatch — an RM that's much smaller/weaker than the policy may not be able to meaningfully discriminate quality among the policy's increasingly sophisticated outputs as training progresses ('reward model can't keep up').
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Rewa.real_example: Anthropic and OpenAI both report training RMs for only a single epoch (or even less) on preference data specifically because additional epochs cause overfitting that manifests as worse downstream PPO behavior — a counterintuitive 'less training is better' finding specific to this component.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.what_it_is: The third and final stage of classic RLHF: use the Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm to fine-tune the SFT model's parameters (now called the 'policy') so that it generates responses that the reward model (from Step 2) scores highly, while staying close to the original SFT policy via a KL-divergence penalty.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.why_it_exists: The reward model gives a SCALAR signal of response quality, but that signal is not differentiable with respect to the discrete TOKENS the policy generates (you can't directly backpropagate 'this response scored 0.8' through the sampling/argmax that produced the tokens). Reinforcement learning provides the machinery to optimize a policy toward maximizing a non-differentiable, sequence-level reward signal via policy-gradient methods.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.how_it_works: For each training prompt: (1) the current policy generates a response (a 'rollout'); (2) the reward model scores the (prompt, response) pair; (3) a KL penalty term is subtracted from this reward, measuring how much the current policy's output distribution has diverged from the reference (SFT) model's distribution for this prompt — discouraging large jumps; (4) PPO updates the policy's weights via gradient ascent on this combined reward signal, using its clipped objective (see PPO clip) to keep individual updates small/stable. This loop repeats over many prompts/batches, gradually shifting the policy toward higher-reward (and KL-constrained) behavior.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.use_when: The final alignment step in the classic RLHF recipe (InstructGPT, LLaMA-2-Chat, early ChatGPT) when you have a working reward model and the infrastructure to run RL training (which involves running the policy, reward model, AND reference model simultaneously — substantial compute).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.avoid_when: PPO-based RLHF is notoriously complex to get right (many hyperparameters, training instability, requires careful tuning of the KL coefficient) and computationally expensive (needs 3-4 models in memory: policy, reference, reward model, and often a value/critic model). Many teams now prefer DPO/GRPO-family methods that achieve similar alignment goals with simpler, more stable training loops and fewer moving parts.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.what_goes_wrong: Training instability — PPO is sensitive to hyperparameters (learning rate, KL coefficient, batch size, number of PPO epochs per batch of rollouts); poorly tuned runs can collapse (policy degenerates to repetitive/nonsensical outputs that happen to score high on a miscalibrated RM) or fail to improve at all. Reward hacking (discussed under KL penalty) is the central failure mode — the policy 'games' the reward model rather than genuinely improving. Compute cost — generating rollouts (full autoregressive generation for every training example, every PPO epoch) is the dominant cost and is much slower than standard supervised gradient steps.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Step.real_example: InstructGPT's RLHF stage used PPO to fine-tune the SFT policy against the learned reward model across ~31k prompts, with careful KL-penalty tuning — the resulting model (InstructGPT/early ChatGPT) showed marked improvements in human-rated helpfulness and instruction-following over the SFT-only model, validating the additional complexity for OpenAI's use case, though the operational complexity is exactly why DPO-family alternatives gained popularity for smaller teams.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|KL p.what_it_is: A regularization term added to the RLHF reward signal that penalizes the policy for diverging (in terms of KL divergence between output distributions) from a fixed reference model (usually the SFT model) — the actual optimization objective is `reward_model_score - β × KL(policy || reference)`.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|KL p.why_it_exists: Without ANY constraint, PPO would happily push the policy toward whatever distribution maximizes the (imperfect, learnable) reward model's score — even if that distribution is degenerate, repetitive, or nonsensical to humans, as long as the RM (mistakenly) scores it highly. The KL penalty acts as a 'leash', ensuring the policy remains a plausible LANGUAGE MODEL (close to the SFT model's distribution) even as it shifts toward higher-reward outputs — trading off reward maximization against staying 'in-distribution'.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|KL p.how_it_works: At each token (or per-sequence), compute the KL divergence between the current policy's output distribution and the frozen reference (SFT) model's distribution for the same context. Subtract β × this KL from the reward model's score to get the effective per-step reward used by PPO. β is a hyperparameter: too small → reward hacking and degenerate outputs (the leash is too loose); too large → the policy barely moves from the SFT model, limiting alignment gains (the leash is too tight). Some implementations adapt β dynamically to target a specific KL budget.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|KL p.use_when: An essential, non-optional component of any PPO-based RLHF setup — without it, RL training reliably degenerates given enough steps, because reward models are never perfect proxies for true human preference.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|KL p.avoid_when: DPO and related methods incorporate an analogous 'implicit KL constraint' directly into their loss function (the DPO loss is derived FROM the same KL-constrained RL objective, just solved in closed form) — so you don't need to separately implement/tune a KL penalty term, though the underlying trade-off (alignment vs. staying close to the reference model) still exists conceptually.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|KL p.what_goes_wrong: Choosing β is one of the most sensitive hyperparameters in RLHF — too low and you get 'reward hacking' failure modes (e.g. the model learns to always express extreme confidence or produce very long responses because the RM happens to rate those highly, regardless of actual correctness/helpfulness); too high and the RLHF stage barely changes the model's behavior, wasting the compute investment. The KL penalty also requires keeping the reference model loaded/running throughout PPO training, adding to the already-substantial memory/compute footprint.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|KL p.real_example: A poorly-tuned (too-low) KL coefficient is a commonly-cited cause of 'mode collapse' in early RLHF experiments, where models would converge to producing the same generic 'safe' response (e.g. always starting with 'I think...' or always hedging with disclaimers) because the reward model happened to score such patterns highly across many prompts, and a weak KL constraint allowed the policy to exploit this uniformly.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Prox.what_it_is: A policy-gradient reinforcement learning algorithm (Schulman et al. 2017) that updates a policy's parameters to increase the probability of actions (here, generated tokens/responses) that led to higher rewards, while constraining each update to be 'proximal' (small) to avoid destructively large policy changes — the standard RL algorithm used in classic RLHF.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Prox.why_it_exists: Vanilla policy-gradient methods can take destructively large steps when an unusually high (or low) reward sample is encountered, causing the policy to change drastically and potentially collapse performance ('falling off a cliff'). PPO was designed as a simpler, more stable alternative to earlier trust-region methods (TRPO) — achieving similar stability guarantees with a much simpler implementation (a clipped objective function instead of complex constrained optimization).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Prox.how_it_works: For each batch of rollouts (generated responses with associated rewards), compute the 'advantage' (how much better/worse this action was than expected, often via a learned value/critic function). Compute the probability ratio between the NEW policy and the OLD policy (before this update) for the actions taken. The PPO objective takes the MINIMUM of (ratio × advantage) and (clipped_ratio × advantage) — this clipping means that once the ratio moves too far from 1 (the policy has changed 'too much' for this action), further increases to the objective from that action are capped, preventing the update from being dominated by a few high-advantage-but-now-overweighted samples. Multiple gradient steps (epochs) are taken on each batch of rollouts before generating new rollouts.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Prox.use_when: The RL algorithm of choice for classic RLHF when reward signals come from a learned reward model and you need stable training over many iterations of policy updates.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Prox.avoid_when: PPO requires a value/critic network (adding more parameters and complexity), careful hyperparameter tuning (clip range, number of epochs per batch, GAE lambda for advantage estimation), and is generally considered among the more complex RL algorithms to get right for LLM fine-tuning — GRPO (used in DeepSeek-R1) was specifically designed to ELIMINATE the value network by estimating advantages via group-relative comparisons, simplifying this.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Prox.what_goes_wrong: Value function estimation errors propagate into advantage estimates, which propagate into policy updates — a poorly-trained value/critic network is a common silent cause of unstable PPO training. The clip range (epsilon, often 0.1-0.2) is a sensitive hyperparameter — too small slows learning excessively, too large reduces the stability benefits PPO is designed to provide. Implementation bugs in LLM-RLHF-PPO (e.g. incorrect handling of padding tokens in the loss, incorrect reward normalization) are notoriously common and hard to detect because training can still 'look like it's working' (loss curves moving) while producing a degraded model.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Prox.real_example: TRL (HuggingFace's Transformer Reinforcement Learning library) provides a `PPOTrainer` that implements this loop for LLMs — managing the policy, reference model, reward model, and value head together; even with a mature library, practitioners report PPO-based RLHF runs requiring substantially more tuning/debugging than DPO runs for comparable preference datasets, which is a major reason DPO-family methods have become the default for most teams.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|PPO.what_it_is: The core mathematical mechanism of PPO: the objective function `min(r(θ)·A, clip(r(θ), 1-ε, 1+ε)·A)`, where r(θ) is the probability ratio between the new and old policy for a given action, A is the advantage estimate, and ε is a small constant (e.g. 0.2) — this clipping caps how much a single update can change the policy's behavior for any given sample.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|PPO.why_it_exists: Without clipping, a sample with a very large advantage estimate (the action turned out much better/worse than expected) combined with a large probability ratio change could dominate the gradient update, causing the policy to overfit to that one sample and potentially destabilize training for all other behaviors. The clip creates a 'trust region' implicitly — beyond a certain amount of policy change for a given action, additional changes don't further increase the objective, so the optimizer has no incentive to push the ratio further in that direction.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|PPO.how_it_works: For each action (token/response) in a training batch: compute r(θ) = π_new(action|state) / π_old(action|state) — how much more/less likely the new policy is to take this action compared to the policy that GENERATED this rollout. If the advantage A is positive (the action was better than expected), the objective is min(r·A, clip(r, 1-ε, 1+ε)·A) — once r exceeds 1+ε, the clipped term caps further reward from increasing r more. If A is negative (action was worse than expected), the clipping works symmetrically in the other direction (capping how much r can DECREASE before the clipped term takes over). The min() ensures the objective is always a pessimistic (lower) bound, discouraging the optimizer from exploiting large ratio changes.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|PPO.use_when: This is the defining mathematical feature of PPO — anytime you're using PPO (vs. vanilla policy gradient or TRPO), this clipping IS the algorithm's stability mechanism; there's no separate 'opt-in' decision.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|PPO.avoid_when: N/A as a standalone choice — but the clip range ε is a hyperparameter you DO need to tune (commonly 0.1-0.3); too aggressive clipping (small ε) over-constrains learning, too loose (large ε) approaches vanilla policy gradient's instability.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|PPO.what_goes_wrong: If most samples in a batch have ratios that exceed the clip range, the EFFECTIVE gradient signal from those samples becomes zero (clipped), meaning the optimizer is essentially not learning from them — this can happen if the policy is changing too fast relative to how often rollouts are refreshed (too many gradient epochs per batch of rollouts), silently stalling learning while loss curves may still look 'active'.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|PPO.real_example: With ε=0.2, if an action had advantage A=+1 and the new/old probability ratio r=1.5 (the new policy is 50% more likely to take this action), the clipped term caps the effective contribution as if r=1.2 (1+ε) — the optimizer 'sees' no additional benefit from r exceeding 1.2 for this sample, preventing runaway reinforcement of that single action even if it happened to have a large measured advantage.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Cons.what_it_is: An alignment technique (Anthropic, 2022) where a model is trained to critique and revise its own outputs according to a written set of principles (a 'constitution'), and this self-critique process is used to generate training data for both SFT and a preference-based RL stage (RLAIF — RL from AI Feedback) — reducing reliance on human-labeled harmful-content examples.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Cons.why_it_exists: Collecting human feedback on harmful/unsafe model outputs requires humans to be EXPOSED to (and produce) harmful content, which is costly, distressing for labelers, and doesn't scale well. Constitutional AI lets the MODEL ITSELF (guided by explicit written principles) identify problems with its own outputs and revise them — turning a small set of human-written PRINCIPLES into a scalable source of training signal, without requiring per-example human labels for harmfulness.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Cons.how_it_works: Two phases: (1) Supervised phase — the model generates a response to a (potentially harmful) prompt, then is prompted to CRITIQUE its own response against a set of constitutional principles (e.g. 'is this response harmful, unethical, or inappropriate?'), then REVISE the response based on the critique; the (prompt, revised response) pairs become SFT data. (2) RL phase (RLAIF) — instead of human preference labels, an AI model evaluates pairs of responses according to the constitution to produce preference labels, which train a reward model exactly as in RLHF, followed by PPO. The 'constitution' is a relatively short list of natural-language principles (e.g. drawn from the UN Declaration of Human Rights, app store guidelines, etc.).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Cons.use_when: Scaling harmlessness/safety alignment beyond what human-labeled preference data can practically cover, or when you want alignment behavior to be traceable to an explicit, auditable set of written principles rather than implicit patterns in human labels.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Cons.avoid_when: For alignment dimensions where human preferences are nuanced/contextual and hard to capture in written principles (e.g. subtle tone/style preferences, humor, domain-specific quality judgments), human feedback remains more reliable than AI-generated feedback against a generic constitution. Also, the AI-feedback process is bounded by the CRITIQUING model's own capabilities — it can't catch failures it itself can't recognize.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Cons.what_goes_wrong: AI feedback can inherit and even AMPLIFY the critiquing model's own biases/blind spots — if the model systematically fails to recognize a certain type of harm, RLAIF based on its judgments won't fix that category. The quality of the 'constitution' itself becomes a critical, somewhat opaque design choice — principles that are too vague produce inconsistent critiques, while overly specific principles may not generalize to novel situations.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|RLHF|Cons.real_example: Anthropic's Claude models use Constitutional AI principles (combined with human feedback) as part of their alignment training — the publicly-documented constitution includes principles like avoiding responses that could be used to cause harm, respecting autonomy, and being helpful, and the self-critique/revision process is part of why Claude can often explain WHY it's declining a request by reference to identifiable principles rather than an opaque learned refusal.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_it_is: Direct Preference Optimization (Rafailov et al. 2023): a method that fine-tunes a language model directly on preference pairs (chosen vs. rejected responses) using a simple classification-style loss, achieving the same alignment objective as RLHF WITHOUT training a separate reward model or running RL/PPO.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.why_it_exists: RLHF's reward-model + PPO pipeline is complex, unstable, and resource-intensive (requires running 3-4 models simultaneously: policy, reference, reward model, value model). DPO derives a mathematical reformulation showing that the OPTIMAL policy under the same KL-constrained reward-maximization objective can be expressed directly in terms of the policy's own log-probabilities relative to a reference model — eliminating the need for an explicit reward model and the RL loop entirely, turning alignment into a simple supervised fine-tuning-like procedure.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.how_it_works: Given a dataset of (prompt, chosen_response, rejected_response) triples, DPO's loss increases the relative log-probability of the chosen response vs. the rejected response, AS MEASURED RELATIVE TO a frozen reference model (usually the SFT checkpoint): loss = -log(sigmoid(β × [(log π(chosen) - log π_ref(chosen)) - (log π(rejected) - log π_ref(rejected))])). The β hyperparameter controls how strongly to deviate from the reference model (analogous to the KL coefficient in RLHF). Training is a straightforward supervised loop — no rollouts, no reward model, no value network.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.use_when: The default choice for most teams doing preference-based alignment today — when you have (or can construct) preference pairs and want RLHF-like alignment benefits with dramatically simpler, more stable training infrastructure (just need the policy + a frozen reference copy).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.avoid_when: If your preference data is purely OFFLINE/static and doesn't reflect the CURRENT policy's outputs, DPO can be less sample-efficient than online RL methods that generate fresh rollouts from the current policy — for tasks where online exploration matters significantly (e.g. complex reasoning where the policy's current failure modes evolve during training), GRPO/online-RL methods may have an edge. Also, DPO can overfit/degenerate (push chosen probability up and rejected down by making BOTH less likely in absolute terms) if not carefully regularized.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_goes_wrong: DPO can suffer from a failure mode where the model decreases the probability of BOTH chosen and rejected responses (it's a relative/contrastive objective, so 'chosen relatively more likely than rejected' can be satisfied even if chosen's absolute probability also drops) — this can degrade general fluency/likelihood of valid responses if not monitored. Out-of-distribution preference data (pairs generated by a very different model than the one being trained) can transfer poorly, since DPO's implicit reward is calibrated relative to the CURRENT policy's reference distribution.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.real_example: Many popular open fine-tunes (e.g. Zephyr, various LLaMA/Mistral community fine-tunes) use DPO on datasets like UltraFeedback (large-scale AI-generated preference pairs) as a final alignment step after SFT — achieving strong chat/instruction-following benchmarks with a fraction of the RLHF pipeline's complexity, which is why DPO became the de facto standard for open-model alignment.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_it_is: The mathematical derivation underlying DPO: starting from the SAME KL-constrained reward-maximization objective that RLHF optimizes via PPO, DPO shows that the optimal policy π* has a closed-form relationship to the reward function and reference policy — `r(x,y) = β log(π*(y|x) / π_ref(y|x)) + const` — which can be substituted into the Bradley-Terry preference model to get a loss expressed purely in terms of policy log-probabilities, with the reward model and RL optimization eliminated algebraically.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.why_it_exists: RLHF's two-stage process (fit a reward model to preferences, then RL-optimize a policy against that reward model under a KL constraint) is solving for the same underlying optimal policy that DPO's closed-form expression characterizes directly. The DPO derivation exists to show these are MATHEMATICALLY EQUIVALENT under the Bradley-Terry preference model assumption — so instead of the two-step 'fit reward model → RL against it' process, you can substitute and get ONE supervised loss that implicitly defines the same reward function via the policy's own probabilities.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.how_it_works: Take the Bradley-Terry preference probability P(chosen > rejected) = sigmoid(r(chosen) - r(rejected)). Substitute the closed-form expression for r(x,y) in terms of π and π_ref (from the KL-constrained RL optimum). The reward terms become differences of log-probability-ratios: r(chosen) - r(rejected) = β[(log π(chosen)/π_ref(chosen)) - (log π(rejected)/π_ref(rejected))]. This expression — purely a function of the POLICY being trained and the FROZEN reference policy — becomes the DPO loss's argument to the sigmoid, with NO separate reward model parameters anywhere.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.use_when: Understanding this derivation helps explain WHY DPO works and what its β hyperparameter means (it plays exactly the role of the KL coefficient in RLHF) — useful when debugging DPO training or explaining the relationship between DPO and RLHF in interviews/discussions.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.avoid_when: The derivation relies on the Bradley-Terry model assumption for preferences (pairwise comparisons reflect an underlying scalar reward) — for preference data that doesn't fit this assumption well (e.g. unpaired binary feedback, as KTO addresses, or multi-way rankings), the closed-form equivalence doesn't directly apply and other methods (KTO, listwise approaches) may be more appropriate.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_goes_wrong: A subtle implication of the derivation: the IMPLICIT reward DPO optimizes is only well-defined RELATIVE TO the chosen reference model π_ref — if π_ref is a poor starting point (e.g. an undertrained SFT model), the 'reward landscape' DPO is implicitly optimizing against may not align well with true human preferences, since the closed-form relationship is anchored to that specific reference.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.real_example: This equivalence is why DPO papers/implementations always require a REFERENCE model (a frozen copy of the SFT checkpoint) alongside the policy being trained — even though there's no explicit 'reward model' or 'RL' in the code, the reference model's log-probabilities play the mathematical role that the reward model + KL penalty played in PPO-based RLHF.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_it_is: Group Relative Policy Optimization: an RL algorithm (introduced in DeepSeekMath, popularized by DeepSeek-R1) that removes PPO's separate value/critic network by estimating the advantage of each response RELATIVE TO A GROUP of other responses sampled for the same prompt — using the group's mean reward as the baseline.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.why_it_exists: PPO requires training a value network (predicting expected future reward) to compute advantages — this adds significant memory/compute overhead (roughly doubling the model footprint, since the value network is often as large as the policy) and is itself a source of training instability if the value estimates are poor. GRPO observes that for many tasks (especially math/reasoning with verifiable rewards), you can sample MULTIPLE responses to the same prompt and use their RELATIVE rewards as a natural baseline — eliminating the value network entirely.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.how_it_works: For each prompt, sample a GROUP of G responses (e.g. G=16 or 64) from the current policy. Compute a reward for each (e.g. 1 if the final answer is correct, 0 if not, for verifiable math/code tasks — RLVR). Compute the advantage for each response as its reward normalized relative to the group's mean and standard deviation (e.g. (r_i - mean(r)) / std(r)) — responses better than the group average get positive advantage, worse get negative, with NO separate value network needed. Apply PPO's clipped objective using these group-relative advantages, plus a KL penalty to a reference model.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.use_when: Particularly effective for REASONING tasks with VERIFIABLE rewards (math problems with checkable answers, code that can be tested) where sampling many responses per prompt and checking correctness is cheap/automatic — this is the core RL recipe behind DeepSeek-R1's reasoning capabilities.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.avoid_when: For tasks where rewards come from a learned/subjective reward model (rather than a cheap verifier) and sampling many responses per prompt is expensive (e.g. requires human evaluation), the group-sampling requirement (multiple generations per prompt) multiplies inference cost during training — may not be worth it vs. DPO if you already have static preference pairs.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_goes_wrong: Group size matters — too small a group gives noisy/high-variance advantage estimates (the 'baseline' from a tiny group is unreliable); too large increases the per-step compute cost (G generations per prompt). If ALL responses in a group get the same reward (e.g. all correct or all wrong for a given prompt), the normalized advantages become degenerate (zero or undefined variance) — some implementations handle this with care (e.g. filtering such groups).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.real_example: DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained using GRPO with purely rule-based rewards (correctness on math/code problems with verifiable answers, plus format rewards for using <think> tags) starting from a base model with NO SFT — demonstrating that GRPO's group-relative signal alone, on verifiable tasks, could elicit sophisticated chain-of-thought reasoning behaviors, which became a template for subsequent 'reasoning model' training (RLVR).

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_it_is: Two additional preference-optimization methods that address specific limitations of DPO: IPO (Identity Preference Optimization, Azar et al. 2023) replaces DPO's loss to avoid overfitting/degeneration on deterministic preferences; KTO (Kahneman-Tversky Optimization, Ethayarajh et al. 2024) optimizes directly from UNPAIRED binary feedback (a single response labeled 'good' or 'bad', not pairs) inspired by prospect theory.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.why_it_exists: DPO assumes you have PAIRED preference data (chosen vs. rejected for the SAME prompt) following a Bradley-Terry model, and its loss can theoretically push toward overfitting when preferences are deterministic (probability of preference = 1, i.e. no noise). IPO reformulates the objective (using a different loss function, e.g. a squared-loss form) that has provably bounded behavior even with deterministic preferences, avoiding DPO's tendency to drive the policy to extreme log-probability ratios. KTO exists because PAIRED preference data is often unavailable or expensive — but UNPAIRED feedback ('this single response was good' or 'this single response was bad', e.g. from thumbs up/down in production) is abundant and cheap, and KTO can learn directly from this without needing matched pairs.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.how_it_works: IPO: replaces DPO's logistic loss (which can push log-probability differences to infinity for deterministic preferences) with a loss that has a finite optimum (e.g. squaring the difference from a target margin), bounding how far the policy diverges from the reference even on 'easy' (high-confidence) preference pairs. KTO: based on prospect theory's idea that humans perceive gains/losses asymmetrically relative to a reference point — for each (prompt, response, label∈{good,bad}) example (no pairing needed), KTO's loss increases the policy's relative log-probability (vs. reference) for 'good' examples and decreases it for 'bad' examples, with different loss curvatures for gains vs. losses reflecting loss-aversion.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.use_when: IPO: when DPO training shows signs of over-optimization/degeneration (policy log-probabilities for chosen/rejected diverging to extremes) and you want a more conservative, bounded objective. KTO: when you only have UNPAIRED binary feedback (thumbs up/down logs, single-response quality ratings) rather than curated preference pairs — common in production systems collecting implicit user feedback at scale.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.avoid_when: If you have clean, well-paired preference data and DPO is training stably, there's often no need to switch to IPO — the practical difference is usually modest. KTO requires careful handling of CLASS IMBALANCE (production thumbs-up/down data is often heavily skewed toward one label) and the theoretical prospect-theory framing requires tuning desirable/undesirable loss weights to compensate.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_goes_wrong: KTO's unpaired nature means it can't directly learn 'A is better than B' relationships, only 'A is good/bad in isolation' — this can be a weaker signal for tasks where RELATIVE quality (vs. absolute quality) is what matters. Both methods, like DPO, depend on a frozen reference model, and their behavior is sensitive to how well that reference model represents a 'reasonable' starting policy.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.real_example: HuggingFace's TRL library implements both `IPOTrainer`-style configurations (via a loss-type flag in DPOTrainer) and `KTOTrainer` — teams with large volumes of production thumbs-up/down feedback (but no paired comparisons) commonly reach for KTO since restructuring such data into matched pairs for DPO would discard most of the signal.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_it_is: A fine-tuning technique where you generate MULTIPLE candidate responses per prompt from a model, filter (reject) the lower-quality ones using some scoring criterion (a reward model, a verifier, or human/LLM judgment), and fine-tune the model (via standard SFT) on the BEST remaining responses — effectively bootstrapping better training data from the model's own outputs.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.why_it_exists: It's a simple way to improve a model using a reward signal WITHOUT any RL machinery (no PPO, no policy gradients, no KL penalties) — just sample-filter-finetune, reusing the standard SFT pipeline. It's particularly attractive when you have a good way to SCORE/VERIFY outputs (a reward model, unit tests for code, answer-checking for math) but want to avoid RL's complexity.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.how_it_works: 1. For each prompt in a dataset, sample K responses from the current model (with temperature > 0 for diversity). 2. Score each response (reward model score, or pass/fail on a verifier like unit tests for code, or correctness check for math). 3. Keep only the best response(s) per prompt (e.g. highest-scoring, or the first one that passes verification — 'best-of-K'). 4. Fine-tune the model (SFT) on these (prompt, best_response) pairs. This can be iterated — fine-tune, then re-sample with the improved model, re-filter, fine-tune again.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.use_when: Tasks with cheap, reliable automatic verification (math with checkable final answers, code with executable tests) where 'best-of-K sampling + filter + SFT' can bootstrap improvement cheaply. Also useful as a simpler alternative to RLHF/DPO when you want SOME preference-driven improvement without the infrastructure for online RL or even paired preference data.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.avoid_when: If verification/scoring is expensive or unreliable (requires human judgment for every sample), generating K samples per prompt and scoring all of them becomes costly — DPO on existing preference pairs may be more sample-efficient. Also, rejection sampling only IMPROVES toward what the CURRENT model can already sometimes produce (it can't generate genuinely novel capabilities the model never samples) — it's an amplification/distillation of the model's own best outputs, not a source of new knowledge.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_goes_wrong: If K (number of samples per prompt) is too small or the model's baseline quality is low, the 'best of K' samples may still be mediocre, and fine-tuning on them won't meaningfully improve the model (garbage in, garbage out, even after filtering). Repeated iterations can lead to a 'feedback loop' where the model becomes increasingly confident in a narrow set of response PATTERNS that happen to score well on the verifier, potentially at the cost of diversity or generalization (similar to mode collapse).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.real_example: LLaMA 2's RLHF pipeline used 'Rejection Sampling fine-tuning' as an intermediate step BEFORE PPO — sampling K outputs per prompt from the current model, selecting the highest-reward-model-scoring response, and fine-tuning on these, iterated across several rounds — providing a cheaper way to make incremental improvements between (more expensive) full PPO training rounds.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_it_is: Self-Play fIne-tuNing (Chen et al. 2024): a method where a model is fine-tuned by treating its OWN previous-iteration outputs as 'rejected' responses and the (human-labeled) SFT dataset's ground-truth responses as 'chosen' — iteratively training the model to distinguish its own generations from the target distribution, framed as a self-play game between successive model checkpoints.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.why_it_exists: DPO and similar methods need preference PAIRS — but collecting human preference pairs is expensive. SPIN observes that if you ALREADY have a high-quality SFT dataset (just (prompt, good_response) pairs, no 'rejected' responses needed), you can construct preference pairs 'for free': the SFT response is the 'chosen' one, and a response SAMPLED FROM THE CURRENT MODEL for the same prompt serves as the 'rejected' one (since the model's current output is presumably 'less good' than the curated SFT target, at least initially) — turning a standard SFT dataset into an iteratively-refreshing preference dataset.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.how_it_works: At iteration t: the current model (π_t) generates a response to each SFT prompt; this generated response is treated as 'rejected', and the SFT dataset's human-written response is 'chosen'. Run DPO-style training on these synthetic pairs to produce π_{t+1} — which should now be 'closer' to the SFT target distribution than π_t was. Repeat: π_{t+1} generates new 'rejected' samples (which should be progressively higher quality as the model improves), and the process continues until the model's own generations become indistinguishable from the SFT target distribution (the 'self-play' converges).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.use_when: When you have a good SFT dataset but lack preference-pair data, and want to extract additional alignment signal from the SFT data itself via iterative self-improvement — particularly useful for further refining a model that's already been through SFT.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.avoid_when: If genuinely diverse, high-quality PREFERENCE data (from real human comparisons or strong external models) is available, it likely provides a richer signal than self-generated 'rejected' samples, which are inherently bounded by the model's own (improving but self-referential) output distribution. Also requires the SFT dataset to be high-quality — SPIN amplifies the model toward matching the SFT distribution, so if that distribution has flaws, SPIN will reinforce them.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_goes_wrong: Since the 'rejected' samples come from the model's OWN generations, as the model improves, the gap between 'chosen' (SFT) and 'rejected' (self-generated) narrows — later iterations provide progressively weaker training signal, and the process can plateau or even become unstable if the model's outputs become too similar to (or sometimes better than, in some dimensions) the SFT targets, confusing the 'which is better' framing.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.real_example: SPIN applied to a 7B model fine-tuned only via SFT on a relatively small instruction dataset showed improvements on benchmarks (MT-Bench, etc.) comparable to models that used additional human-preference-based DPO/RLHF — demonstrating that the SFT dataset itself, used iteratively via self-play, contains additional 'free' alignment signal beyond what a single SFT pass extracts.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_it_is: RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards): training paradigm behind 'reasoning models' (OpenAI o1/o3, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini 'Thinking' models) where RL (typically GRPO-style) is applied using REWARDS THAT ARE AUTOMATICALLY VERIFIABLE — e.g. 'is the final numeric answer correct?' for math, 'do the unit tests pass?' for code — rather than rewards from a learned/subjective reward model, encouraging the model to develop long, effective internal chain-of-thought reasoning ('thinking') before producing a final answer.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.why_it_exists: Learned reward models (as in classic RLHF) are imperfect proxies for quality and are exploitable (reward hacking) — but for tasks with OBJECTIVELY CHECKABLE answers (math problems with known solutions, code with test suites, logic puzzles with verifiable solutions), you can define a reward function that's essentially ground-truth (correct=1, incorrect=0), with NO reward-model approximation error. RLVR exploits this: at scale, training a model to maximize this ground-truth-verifiable reward (via RL) elicits emergent long-form reasoning ('thinking out loud' at length, self-correction, exploring multiple approaches) because longer/more careful reasoning chains correlate with higher success rates on hard problems.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.how_it_works: Curate a large dataset of problems with VERIFIABLE correct answers (math competition problems, coding problems with test suites, logic puzzles). For each problem, sample multiple completions from the model (often within a <think>...</think> reasoning block followed by a final answer). Compute reward = 1 if the final answer matches the verified solution (or passes tests), 0 otherwise — plus often small auxiliary rewards for format compliance (e.g. using the thinking-tag structure). Run RL (GRPO or similar) to maximize this reward across many problems and samples. Over training, the model's reasoning chains tend to grow longer and more sophisticated (self-verification, backtracking, trying alternative approaches) — these behaviors EMERGE from the RL process rather than being explicitly demonstrated/imitated.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.use_when: Building or fine-tuning models for domains with objectively verifiable tasks — competition math, programming/code-with-tests, formal logic, certain scientific QA — where RLVR has produced dramatic capability jumps (DeepSeek-R1's reasoning benchmarks rival/exceed much larger non-reasoning models on math/code).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.avoid_when: For open-ended tasks without a verifiable ground truth (creative writing, subjective Q&A, general conversation), RLVR has no natural reward signal — these still rely on learned reward models / human preferences (RLHF/DPO-style), or RLVR is combined with those methods for a hybrid approach. Also, RLVR-trained 'reasoning' models tend to produce much LONGER outputs (more 'thinking' tokens) — increasing latency/cost for tasks that don't need deep reasoning.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.what_goes_wrong: RLVR can lead to 'reward hacking' even with verifiable rewards in subtle ways — e.g. a model might learn to produce reasoning that LOOKS like careful step-by-step work but is partially post-hoc rationalization of an answer reached via shortcuts/pattern-matching, especially if the training distribution has exploitable patterns (memorized answer formats for common problem types). The dramatically increased output length (sometimes thousands of 'thinking' tokens for simple questions) significantly raises inference cost/latency — and current reasoning models sometimes apply this expensive 'deep thinking' even to trivial questions that don't need it, an over-thinking problem labs actively try to mitigate.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|Preferenc.real_example: DeepSeek-R1-Zero, trained purely via GRPO-based RLVR on verifiable math/code rewards starting from a base model (no SFT), spontaneously developed behaviors like generating very long chains of thought, re-examining and revising its own earlier steps ('Wait, let me reconsider...'), and exploring multiple solution approaches before committing to a final answer — none of which were explicitly demonstrated in training data, illustrating how a simple verifiable-reward RL signal can elicit complex emergent reasoning strategies.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_it_is: Low-Rank Adaptation (Hu et al. 2021): a PEFT method that freezes all original model weights W and instead learns a small additive update ΔW = B·A, where B (d×r) and A (r×k) are low-rank matrices with rank r much less than d, k — drastically reducing the number of trainable parameters while approximating the effect of fine-tuning the full weight matrix.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.why_it_exists: Full fine-tuning updates every parameter (billions for modern LLMs), requiring storage for full gradients and optimizer states per parameter — prohibitively memory-intensive. Empirically, the WEIGHT UPDATES needed to adapt a pretrained model to a new task tend to have low 'intrinsic rank' — i.e. ΔW can be well-approximated by a low-rank decomposition. LoRA exploits this: instead of learning a full d×k update matrix, learn two much smaller matrices whose product approximates it.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.how_it_works: For a weight matrix W (d×k), LoRA adds W + ΔW = W + B·A, where B is d×r and A is r×k, with r (e.g. 8, 16, 64) much less than min(d,k). Only A and B are trained; W stays frozen. A is typically initialized to small random values and B to zero, so ΔW=0 at the start of training (the model behaves identically to the base model initially). During training, gradients flow only through A and B — the number of trainable parameters is r×(d+k) instead of d×k, often a >100x reduction. At inference, ΔW can either be added to W (merged, zero extra latency) or kept separate (allowing multiple LoRA adapters to be swapped for different tasks on the same base model).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.use_when: The default choice for fine-tuning large models on consumer/limited hardware, for task-specific adapters that can be swapped in/out, or when you want to fine-tune multiple specialized variants of the same base model without storing multiple full copies.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.avoid_when: For tasks requiring very large behavioral shifts (e.g. teaching a model an entirely new language or fundamentally different capability), low-rank updates may not have enough capacity — full fine-tuning or continued pretraining may be needed. Also, if you need the absolute maximum quality and have the compute budget, full fine-tuning can still edge out LoRA on some benchmarks.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_goes_wrong: Choosing rank r too low can underfit (the model can't capture the needed adaptation); too high approaches full fine-tuning's cost/overfitting risk without proportional benefit. Which layers/modules to apply LoRA to (attention projections vs. MLP layers vs. all linear layers) significantly affects results and is often under-explored — defaulting to only attention q/v projections (the original paper's choice) may leave performance on the table for some tasks vs. applying LoRA to all linear layers.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.real_example: Fine-tuning LLaMA-2-7B with LoRA rank 16 on attention projections trains roughly 4-8 million parameters out of 7 billion (~0.1%) — fitting comfortably on a single consumer GPU (e.g. 24GB) where full fine-tuning would require 80GB+ multi-GPU setups, while achieving comparable task-specific performance on many benchmarks.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_it_is: A concrete illustration of LoRA's parameter efficiency: for typical configurations (rank r=8-16 applied to attention projection matrices of a 7B-70B parameter model), the number of TRAINABLE parameters is roughly 0.01%-0.5% of the total model size — meaning 99.5%+ of the model's weights remain completely unchanged during fine-tuning.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.why_it_exists: This extreme efficiency is what makes LoRA practical on consumer hardware and enables a whole ecosystem of lightweight, swappable 'adapters' — a marketplace of small (megabytes, not gigabytes) LoRA files that can each specialize a shared base model for a different task/style/domain.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.how_it_works: For a weight matrix of size d×k (e.g. 4096×4096 in a 7B model's attention projection), full fine-tuning updates 4096×4096 ≈ 16.8M parameters for JUST that matrix. With LoRA rank r=8, you instead train two matrices of size 4096×8 and 8×4096 = 65,536 parameters each, totaling ~131K — about 0.78% of that matrix's parameters, and when applied to only a subset of matrices across the model, the OVERALL trainable fraction often lands around 0.1-1% depending on rank and target modules.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.use_when: This efficiency is the reason LoRA is the default for: storing many task-specific adapters cheaply (each adapter might be 10-100MB vs. the base model's 10-100GB+), rapid experimentation (faster training steps, less memory pressure allows larger batch sizes), and serving multiple fine-tuned 'personalities' from one base model deployment.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.avoid_when: If the downstream serving infrastructure can't easily support 'base model + swappable adapter' architectures (some deployment setups prefer a single merged model), the storage/deployment benefits of small adapter files may not translate into operational simplicity — merging LoRA weights into the base model (producing a full-size model) negates the storage advantage, though it can simplify serving (no adapter-loading logic needed).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_goes_wrong: Because so few parameters are updated, LoRA models can sometimes 'plateau' on tasks needing substantial new capability — practitioners sometimes mistakenly increase rank dramatically (e.g. r=256) assuming more parameters always helps, when often the LIMITING factor is which layers receive adapters or the quality/quantity of training data, not raw trainable-parameter count.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.real_example: HuggingFace Hub hosts thousands of LoRA adapters for popular base models (LLaMA, Mistral, Stable Diffusion) — each just tens of megabytes, allowing users to download a 50MB adapter and combine it with a shared multi-GB base model to get a specialized model, rather than downloading a separate full multi-GB checkpoint per specialization.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_it_is: Quantized LoRA (Dettmers et al. 2023): a technique that combines LoRA with 4-bit quantization of the FROZEN base model — the base model's weights are stored/computed in 4-bit precision (using the NF4 data type), while the small LoRA adapter matrices are trained in higher precision (bf16), drastically reducing the GPU memory needed for fine-tuning.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.why_it_exists: Even with LoRA's reduced TRAINABLE parameters, the FROZEN base model still needs to be loaded in memory in full/half precision (e.g. a 70B model in fp16 needs ~140GB just for weights) — this alone exceeds consumer GPU memory for large models. QLoRA shows that quantizing the frozen base model to 4-bit (reducing its memory footprint ~4x vs fp16) doesn't meaningfully hurt fine-tuning quality, because the LoRA adapters (trained in higher precision) can compensate for the quantization's small approximation errors.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.how_it_works: The base model is loaded in 4-bit NF4 (NormalFloat4, a data type designed to better represent normally-distributed weight values than standard int4). LoRA adapter matrices A and B are added on top, trained in bf16. During the forward/backward pass, 4-bit weights are de-quantized on-the-fly to bf16 for computation (the LoRA matrices' gradients flow through this de-quantized computation, but only A and B are updated — the base weights remain in their original 4-bit storage). Additional techniques: 'double quantization' (quantizing the quantization constants themselves for extra memory savings) and paged optimizers (using NVIDIA unified memory to handle occasional memory spikes without OOM crashes).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.use_when: Fine-tuning large models (13B-70B+) on a SINGLE consumer or prosumer GPU (e.g. 24-48GB) where even loading the base model in fp16 wouldn't fit, let alone fine-tuning it.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.avoid_when: If you have ample multi-GPU memory and want the absolute best quality with no quantization-related approximation, full-precision LoRA (or full fine-tuning) avoids any quantization noise — though QLoRA's quality gap is typically small (the original paper showed QLoRA fine-tuning matched full 16-bit fine-tuning performance on benchmarks).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_goes_wrong: 4-bit quantization + LoRA training is somewhat slower per-step than full-precision LoRA (due to the de-quantization overhead in each forward/backward pass) — you trade memory for some compute/time. Some non-standard architectures or layer types may not be well-supported by 4-bit quantization libraries (bitsandbytes), requiring fallbacks to fp16 for those components.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.real_example: QLoRA enabled fine-tuning a 65B parameter LLaMA model on a SINGLE 48GB GPU (previously requiring 780GB+ for full fine-tuning) while matching the performance of full 16-bit fine-tuning on instruction-following benchmarks — this dramatically democratized large-model fine-tuning, and is the technique behind most 'fine-tune a 70B model on your laptop/single-GPU-cloud-instance' tutorials.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_it_is: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (Liu et al. 2024): a PEFT method that decomposes a pretrained weight matrix W into its MAGNITUDE (a scalar per column, ||W||) and DIRECTION (the normalized weight matrix W/||W||) components, then applies LoRA-style low-rank updates only to the DIRECTION while separately learning the magnitude — more closely mimicking how full fine-tuning updates weights.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.why_it_exists: Analysis comparing LoRA updates to full fine-tuning updates found that LoRA tends to change magnitude and direction of weights in a CORRELATED way, whereas full fine-tuning can change them more INDEPENDENTLY — this difference may explain part of the quality gap between LoRA and full fine-tuning. DoRA's decomposition gives the model more flexibility to adjust magnitude and direction somewhat independently, better approximating full fine-tuning's update patterns while keeping LoRA's parameter efficiency.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.how_it_works: Decompose each pretrained weight matrix W = m × (V / ||V||), where m is a (learnable) magnitude vector and V/||V|| is the unit-normalized direction. Apply LoRA's low-rank update (B·A) to the DIRECTION component V (i.e. V' = V + B·A), then re-derive the new direction (V'/||V'||) and combine with the (separately trained) magnitude vector m to get the final weight: W' = m × (V'/||V'||). Both the LoRA matrices (A, B) and the magnitude vector m are trainable; the base direction V is frozen (just like W is frozen in standard LoRA).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.use_when: When LoRA fine-tuning underperforms full fine-tuning on a task and you want a 'drop-in' improvement that keeps similar parameter efficiency — DoRA adds only a small number of extra trainable parameters (the magnitude vectors) compared to standard LoRA.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.avoid_when: DoRA adds slight implementation/computational complexity (the decomposition and renormalization steps) compared to vanilla LoRA — if LoRA is already meeting your quality bar, the marginal gains may not justify the added complexity. Also less battle-tested/widely-supported across all PEFT library integrations compared to standard LoRA at time of newer adoption.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_goes_wrong: The decomposition adds a small computational overhead during training (normalization operations) — generally negligible but worth being aware of for very large-scale training. As with all LoRA variants, choice of rank and target modules still matters and DoRA doesn't eliminate the need for that tuning.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.real_example: The DoRA paper reports consistent improvements over standard LoRA across several benchmarks (commonsense reasoning, visual instruction tuning) at the SAME parameter count, and HuggingFace's PEFT library added DoRA as a configuration option (`use_dora=True` in LoraConfig) — making it an easy swap-in for teams already using LoRA via PEFT.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_it_is: Adaptive LoRA (Zhang et al. 2023): a PEFT method that dynamically allocates DIFFERENT ranks to different weight matrices/layers during training, based on each matrix's estimated 'importance' to the task — instead of using a single fixed rank r for all LoRA adapters across the model.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.why_it_exists: Standard LoRA applies the SAME rank to every adapted matrix, implicitly assuming all layers/matrices need the same amount of adaptation capacity. In reality, some layers (e.g. certain attention heads or later layers) may need more adaptation for a given task than others. AdaLoRA aims to spend the 'parameter budget' more efficiently by giving important matrices higher effective rank and less important ones lower rank, within the same total parameter budget as a fixed-rank baseline.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.how_it_works: Parameterize each LoRA update as a SVD-like decomposition (ΔW = P·Λ·Q, where Λ is a diagonal matrix of 'singular values'). During training, periodically compute IMPORTANCE SCORES for each singular value/triplet (based on sensitivity — how much the loss would change if that component were removed) and PRUNE the lowest-importance components, effectively reducing the rank of less-important matrices while preserving (or reallocating budget to) more important ones — iteratively redistributing a fixed total-rank budget across the model's matrices based on observed importance during training.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.use_when: When you want to extract more performance from a fixed parameter budget by letting training itself determine where adaptation capacity is most needed — useful for research/optimization-focused fine-tuning where squeezing out extra benchmark points matters.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.avoid_when: Adds training-time complexity (importance scoring, pruning schedule, additional hyperparameters for the pruning schedule) compared to fixed-rank LoRA — for most practical fine-tuning tasks, the gains may not justify this complexity, and fixed-rank LoRA/QLoRA remains far more commonly used in practice due to simplicity and tooling support.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_goes_wrong: The importance-scoring and pruning schedule introduce additional hyperparameters (how often to prune, target final rank distribution, warm-up steps before pruning starts) that need tuning — a poorly-tuned schedule can prune important components too early (before they've had a chance to be useful) or too late (wasting the efficiency benefit).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.real_example: AdaLoRA's original experiments showed it could match or exceed fixed-rank LoRA's performance on GLUE benchmark tasks at the SAME total parameter budget by concentrating rank in a subset of matrices — but in practice, most production fine-tuning workflows (and PEFT library defaults) still favor fixed-rank LoRA/QLoRA/DoRA for their simplicity and predictable behavior.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_it_is: A PEFT method (Li & Liang, 2021) that prepends a sequence of trainable, continuous ('soft') vectors — not corresponding to any real tokens — to the input of EVERY transformer layer's keys and values in self-attention, while keeping all original model weights frozen. Only these prefix vectors are trained.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.why_it_exists: An alternative to weight-update-based PEFT (like LoRA): instead of modifying the model's WEIGHTS, prefix tuning modifies the INPUT/ACTIVATIONS by giving the model additional 'virtual tokens' to attend to, which can steer its behavior for a specific task — inspired by how a good natural-language prompt prefix can steer behavior, but using learned continuous vectors instead of discrete words (which can represent task-specific information more flexibly than any actual word/phrase could).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.how_it_works: For each transformer layer, prepend a small number (e.g. 10-200) of trainable vectors to the keys (K) and values (V) used in self-attention — these act as additional 'tokens' that real input tokens can attend to, but they don't correspond to any vocabulary token and are never themselves 'generated'. During training, gradients flow only to these prefix vectors (plus sometimes a small reparameterization MLP that generates them, for training stability); all transformer weights remain frozen. At inference, the prefix is concatenated to K/V at every layer before processing the actual input.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.use_when: Generation tasks (especially with encoder-decoder or decoder-only models for table-to-text, summarization) where the original prefix-tuning paper showed strong results, or when you want a PEFT method that doesn't modify weight matrices at all (useful for certain serving architectures).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.avoid_when: LoRA has largely superseded prefix tuning in popularity for general LLM fine-tuning — prefix tuning can be harder to optimize (the reparameterization MLP adds complexity) and consumes some of the model's context window/attention budget on every input (the prefix tokens take up 'space' that could otherwise be used for actual content), unlike LoRA which adds zero inference-time sequence length.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_goes_wrong: Prefix length is a sensitive hyperparameter — too short limits adaptation capacity, too long eats into the effective context window available for real content and can slow inference (more tokens to attend to at every layer). Direct optimization of prefix vectors (without the reparameterization MLP) was found in the original paper to be unstable/sensitive to initialization — the MLP reparameterization helps but adds its own complexity.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.real_example: P-Tuning v2 (a successor approach) found that prefix-tuning-style methods, when applied across ALL layers (not just the input embedding layer), could match fine-tuning performance across model scales — but in current practice, LoRA/QLoRA's combination of simplicity, zero added inference-time sequence length, and strong tooling support (PEFT library) has made it the dominant choice over prefix tuning for most LLM fine-tuning.

5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_it_is: A PEFT method (Lester et al. 2021) that prepends a small number of trainable continuous vectors ONLY to the INPUT EMBEDDING layer (not to every layer's K/V as in prefix tuning) — these 'soft prompt' embeddings are the ONLY trainable parameters; the entire rest of the model (including all transformer layers) remains frozen.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.why_it_exists: An even more extreme parameter-efficiency point than prefix tuning — by only modifying the INPUT to the model (the embedding sequence), prompt tuning requires the absolute minimum number of trainable parameters (just embedding_dim × prompt_length, often a few thousand to tens of thousands of parameters total) while still allowing task-specific adaptation via the model's existing capacity to 'follow' different input contexts.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.how_it_works: Prepend k learnable embedding vectors (each of dimension = model's hidden size) to the input token embeddings before the first transformer layer. These vectors don't correspond to real vocabulary tokens — they're free parameters initialized randomly or from sampled vocabulary embeddings. During training (standard task loss, e.g. cross-entropy), gradients flow back to update ONLY these k embedding vectors; every transformer layer's weights are completely frozen and unchanged. The model processes [soft_prompt_embeddings, real_input_embeddings] through its normal (frozen) forward pass.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.use_when: Extremely resource-constrained fine-tuning scenarios, or 'soft prompt libraries' where you want to store many task-specific prompts as tiny files (a few KB each) to specialize a single frozen model deployment for many tasks without any model weight changes at all.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.avoid_when: The original paper found prompt tuning's effectiveness GROWS with model scale — for smaller models (sub-billion parameters), prompt tuning significantly underperforms full fine-tuning/LoRA; it only becomes competitive at very large scale (10B+ parameters), where the frozen model already has enough latent capability that a 'steering' input is sufficient. For most practical mid-sized model fine-tuning, LoRA offers better quality per unit of complexity.
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.what_goes_wrong: Optimization can be harder/slower to converge than LoRA — soft prompt embeddings are 'far' (in parameter-update terms) from the model's internal weight computations, so gradient signals are weaker/noisier. Prompt length vs. quality trade-off — longer soft prompts give more capacity but consume context window space, and the original paper found diminishing returns past a certain length (~20-100 tokens depending on task).
5|🔴 T1 Fine-tuning & Alignment|PEFT — Pa.real_example: Google's original prompt tuning paper showed that with a sufficiently large frozen model (T5-XXL, 11B params), prompt tuning could match full fine-tuning performance on SuperGLUE tasks while training literally thousands of times fewer parameters — but for smaller models this gap doesn't close, which is part of why LoRA (effective across a much wider range of model sizes) became more broadly adopted.
