5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Emb.what_it_is: The decision of which embedding model to use for converting text into vectors for a RAG system's vector store — choices include proprietary API models (OpenAI `text-embedding-3-large/small`, Cohere embed), open-source models (BGE, E5, GTE, Sentence-Transformers variants), and considerations like embedding dimensionality, multilingual support, domain specialization, and cost/latency.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Emb.why_it_exists: The embedding model determines what 'similar' means for retrieval — a poorly-matched embedding model (e.g. one not tuned for the domain's vocabulary, or one optimized for a different task like classification rather than retrieval) will retrieve less relevant chunks REGARDLESS of how good the chunking/prompting is, making this one of the highest-leverage choices in a RAG system.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Emb.how_it_works: Embedding models map text to fixed-size dense vectors (e.g. 1536 dimensions for `text-embedding-3-small`) such that semantically similar text maps to nearby vectors (by cosine similarity or dot product). Trade-offs: proprietary API models (OpenAI, Cohere) are easy to use, generally high-quality, but incur per-token cost and require sending data to a third party (a consideration for sensitive data). Open-source models (run locally/self-hosted) avoid per-call cost and data egress but require hosting infrastructure (GPU for fast embedding of large corpora) and may need domain-specific fine-tuning to match proprietary model quality. Higher-dimensional embeddings can capture more nuance but cost more storage/compute for similarity search; some models (e.g. `text-embedding-3` family) support 'shortening' embeddings to reduce dimensionality with graceful quality degradation. The MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) leaderboard is commonly used to compare models' retrieval performance across tasks/languages.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Emb.use_when: Proprietary API embeddings for quick prototyping or when data sensitivity/self-hosting isn't a blocker and convenience matters. Open-source/self-hosted embeddings when data can't leave your infrastructure, when embedding volume is high enough that per-call API costs dominate, or when domain-specific fine-tuning of the embedding model meaningfully improves retrieval for a specialized corpus (legal, medical, code).
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Emb.avoid_when: Don't pick an embedding model purely on MTEB leaderboard rank without considering your SPECIFIC domain/language — a model that's #1 on general benchmarks may underperform a smaller, domain-tuned model on your particular corpus (e.g. code-specific embeddings for a codebase-search RAG system).
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Emb.what_goes_wrong: CHANGING embedding models requires RE-EMBEDDING the entire corpus (old and new embeddings aren't comparable/compatible in the same vector space) — an easy-to-overlook migration cost when iterating on embedding choice. Using a SHORT-CONTEXT embedding model (e.g. max 512 tokens) on chunks that exceed that limit causes silent truncation — only the first part of the chunk gets embedded, and the rest is invisible to retrieval.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Emb.real_example: A team building a RAG system over legal contracts initially uses `text-embedding-3-small` for prototyping (fast, cheap, good general quality), but after evaluation finds that domain-specific legal terminology ('indemnification', 'force majeure') isn't well-distinguished by the general model — switching to a legal-domain-fine-tuned open-source embedding model improves retrieval precision for clause-specific queries, at the cost of needing to self-host the embedding model and re-embed the entire contract corpus.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Vec.what_it_is: The process of storing embedded chunks in a vector database (Chroma, Pinecone, Weaviate, FAISS, pgvector, etc.) along with METADATA (source document, page number, section, date, author, access permissions, etc.) attached to each vector, enabling both similarity search AND structured filtering.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Vec.why_it_exists: Pure vector similarity search alone can't express constraints like 'only search documents from 2024' or 'only search documents this user has access to' — metadata indexing exists to combine the FUZZY matching of embeddings with the PRECISE filtering of traditional database queries, and to preserve provenance information so retrieved chunks can be traced back to their source (for citations, debugging, access control).
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Vec.how_it_works: When chunks are embedded and inserted into the vector store, each vector is stored alongside a metadata dict (e.g. `{'source': 'policy.pdf', 'page': 3, 'department': 'HR', 'date': '2024-01-15'}`). Vector databases support 'filtered search': retrieve the top-k most similar vectors to a query vector, but ONLY among vectors whose metadata matches given filter criteria (e.g. `department == 'HR'`). Indexing strategies (e.g. HNSW — Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs) enable approximate nearest-neighbor search to scale to millions of vectors with sub-linear query time, trading a small amount of recall for large speed gains over exact search.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Vec.use_when: Any production RAG system needs metadata for at least: (1) citing sources in responses (showing users WHERE an answer came from), (2) access control (ensuring users only retrieve documents they're authorized to see), and (3) often filtering by recency/category to narrow the search space and improve relevance.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Vec.avoid_when: For tiny, homogeneous corpora (a handful of documents, all equally relevant/accessible to all users), elaborate metadata schemes add complexity without benefit — simple unfiltered similarity search may suffice.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Vec.what_goes_wrong: Forgetting to enforce metadata-based ACCESS CONTROL in retrieval is a serious security issue — if document permissions exist in the source system but aren't encoded as vector-store metadata filters, a RAG system can retrieve and surface content from documents the querying user shouldn't be able to see, leaking sensitive information across access boundaries. Over-aggressive metadata filtering (e.g. filtering to an overly narrow date range) can filter out the one relevant document, returning empty/poor results even though pure similarity search would have found it.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Vec.real_example: A multi-tenant SaaS RAG system stores `tenant_id` as metadata on every embedded chunk, and EVERY retrieval query includes a mandatory filter `tenant_id == current_user.tenant_id` — ensuring tenant A's documents are never retrievable when tenant B's users query the system, even if their queries are semantically similar to tenant A's content.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Sim.what_it_is: The core retrieval operation in RAG: given a query embedding, find the top-k chunks whose embeddings are most SIMILAR (by cosine similarity, dot product, or Euclidean distance) to the query, OPTIONALLY restricted to chunks matching specified metadata FILTERS (e.g. `source == 'handbook.pdf' AND date > '2024-01-01'`).
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Sim.why_it_exists: Similarity search alone finds SEMANTICALLY relevant content but can't enforce hard constraints (only this user's documents, only this date range, only this document type) — combining vector similarity with structured metadata filtering lets RAG systems narrow the search space to a relevant/authorized SUBSET before (or while) ranking by semantic similarity, improving both relevance and correctness.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Sim.how_it_works: The vector database executes a 'filtered ANN (approximate nearest neighbor) search': it applies the metadata filter to restrict the candidate set, then performs similarity search (often via an index like HNSW) within that restricted set, returning the top-k closest vectors and their associated text/metadata. Implementation varies — some databases apply the filter BEFORE the ANN search (pre-filtering, exact but can be slow if the filter is very restrictive on a large index), others apply it AFTER (post-filtering, fast but may return fewer than k results if many top matches are filtered out).
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Sim.use_when: Whenever retrieval needs to be scoped — by user/tenant (access control), by document type/category (e.g. 'only search FAQs, not internal memos'), by recency (e.g. 'prefer documents from the last 6 months'), or by any other structured attribute relevant to the query.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Sim.avoid_when: When the corpus is small and homogeneous enough that pure similarity search already returns highly relevant results — adding filters when there's nothing meaningful to filter by adds complexity without benefit.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Sim.what_goes_wrong: Post-filtering implementations can silently return FEWER than k results (or zero) if the filter eliminates most/all of the top-k similarity matches — applications need to handle 'not enough results after filtering' gracefully (e.g. by retrieving a larger initial k before filtering). Combining filters incorrectly (e.g. AND vs OR logic errors in filter construction, especially when filters are dynamically built from LLM-generated structured queries as in self-query retrievers) can silently over- or under-restrict results.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Sim.real_example: A customer support RAG system retrieves the top-5 most similar FAQ chunks but filters to `product_line == detected_product AND language == user_language` — ensuring a French-speaking user asking about 'Product B' only receives FAQ content relevant to Product B in French, even if semantically-similar English content about Product A exists in the index.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ret.what_it_is: Legacy LangChain chain classes that bundle the 'retrieve relevant documents, then ask an LLM to answer using them' pattern into a single object: `RetrievalQA` returns just the answer text, while `RetrievalQAWithSourcesChain` additionally returns the SOURCE documents/metadata used to generate the answer, enabling citations.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ret.why_it_exists: These chains existed to provide an out-of-the-box, minimal-code way to stand up a basic RAG question-answering system — wrapping retriever + prompt + LLM + (optionally) source-tracking into one `.run()`/`.invoke()` call, before LCEL became the standard composition mechanism.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ret.how_it_works: `RetrievalQA.from_chain_type(llm, retriever=retriever)` creates a chain that, when given a question, calls the retriever to get relevant documents, formats them into a default (or custom) prompt template along with the question, and calls the LLM, returning the generated answer. `RetrievalQAWithSourcesChain` does the same but ALSO returns the source documents (with their metadata) alongside the answer, and its default prompt instructs the LLM to cite sources in the response, enabling the application to display 'Answer: ... (Sources: doc1.pdf p.3, doc2.pdf p.7)'.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ret.use_when: Historically, for quick RAG prototypes with minimal custom logic. In current LangChain, these are largely SUPERSEDED by LCEL-composed chains (`{'context': retriever, 'question': RunnablePassthrough()} | prompt | llm | parser`), which offer more flexibility (custom prompts, streaming, easier debugging) for similar effort.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ret.avoid_when: For new projects — LCEL composition is now the recommended pattern, offering more transparency into intermediate steps (helpful for debugging via LangSmith) and more flexibility (custom source formatting, conditional logic) than these higher-level pre-packaged chains allow.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ret.what_goes_wrong: These higher-level chains' default prompts/behaviors can be opaque — when results are poor, it's harder to inspect/modify exactly what prompt was constructed compared to an explicit LCEL chain where the prompt template is visible in the code. Source attribution in `RetrievalQAWithSourcesChain` depends on the LLM correctly following citation instructions in the prompt — it can still 'forget' to cite or cite incorrectly, since citation isn't ENFORCED structurally, just prompted.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ret.real_example: An early RAG prototype might use `RetrievalQAWithSourcesChain.from_chain_type(llm, retriever=vectorstore.as_retriever())` to get a working Q&A-with-citations system in 2 lines of code — useful for a quick demo, though a production system would likely migrate to an explicit LCEL chain for more control over prompt design and citation formatting.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.what_it_is: A RAG pattern that accounts for MULTI-TURN conversations — where a user's current question may depend on PRIOR turns (e.g. 'What about for enterprise plans?' following 'What's the pricing for the basic plan?') — by first REFORMULATING the current question into a standalone query (using the conversation history for context) before performing retrieval, then generating an answer using both the retrieved context and the conversation history.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.why_it_exists: Naive RAG embeds and retrieves based on the LATEST user message alone — but follow-up questions are often ambiguous/incomplete without prior context ('what about enterprise?' has no meaning for retrieval without knowing the topic is 'pricing'). Conversational RAG exists to make retrieval AWARE of conversation history, so follow-up questions retrieve relevant documents even when the current message alone is underspecified.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.how_it_works: Typically a TWO-STEP process: (1) a 'history-aware retriever' step takes the chat history + the latest user message and uses an LLM to REWRITE it into a standalone question (e.g. 'What about for enterprise plans?' + history about basic-plan pricing → 'What is the pricing for enterprise plans?'), then performs retrieval using this rewritten query; (2) the retrieved documents, the ORIGINAL chat history, and the latest user message are all passed to the final LLM call to generate a contextually-appropriate answer. LangChain provides `create_history_aware_retriever` and `create_retrieval_chain` helpers for this pattern.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.use_when: Any chatbot/assistant where users naturally ask follow-up questions that reference earlier parts of the conversation — virtually all conversational (as opposed to single-shot Q&A) RAG applications.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.avoid_when: Single-shot Q&A interfaces (search-style, one question per session, no follow-ups) don't need the extra query-rewriting LLM call — it adds latency/cost for no benefit if there's no history to be aware of.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.what_goes_wrong: The query-rewriting step is itself an LLM call that can fail/misinterpret — if it rewrites a follow-up question INCORRECTLY (e.g. conflating two different topics from earlier in the conversation), retrieval will be based on the wrong reformulated query, and the final answer will be off-topic even though the LLM 'sees' the original question too. Long conversation histories passed into the rewriting step face the same context-window/cost concerns as any conversational memory — may need summarization or windowing for very long conversations.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.real_example: A documentation chatbot: user asks 'How do I configure SSL?', gets an answer about SSL configuration; user follows up with 'and for the staging environment?' — the history-aware retriever rewrites this to 'How do I configure SSL for the staging environment?', retrieves staging-specific SSL documentation (which a naive retrieval on 'and for the staging environment?' alone would likely miss), and the final LLM call produces a relevant follow-up answer.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Mul.what_it_is: A retrieval technique where an LLM generates SEVERAL different phrasings/variants of the user's original query, retrieval is performed for EACH variant separately, and the (deduplicated) UNION of retrieved documents across all variants is used as the final context.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Mul.why_it_exists: A single query embedding may not be close to the embeddings of all relevant documents — different phrasings of the 'same' underlying information need ('What's our refund policy?' vs 'Can customers get their money back?' vs 'How do returns work?') can have meaningfully different embeddings and retrieve DIFFERENT relevant chunks. Multi-query retrieval exists to increase RECALL by casting a 'wider net' — querying from multiple semantic angles rather than relying on a single embedding to be close to everything relevant.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Mul.how_it_works: An LLM is prompted with the original query and asked to generate N (e.g. 3-5) alternative phrasings/related questions. Each variant (including the original) is embedded and used to retrieve top-k documents independently. The retrieved document sets are UNIONED and deduplicated (since different query variants often retrieve overlapping documents), producing a larger, more diverse candidate pool than single-query retrieval — this pool may then be passed directly to the LLM or further filtered/reranked.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Mul.use_when: Queries where users phrase requests in ways that may not closely match the vocabulary/phrasing used in the source documents — common in domains with jargon mismatches between how users ASK and how documents are WRITTEN (e.g. casual user language vs formal documentation language).
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Mul.avoid_when: Adds latency (LLM call to generate variants) and cost (multiple retrieval calls + larger context) — for queries that already retrieve well with single-query retrieval, or in latency-sensitive applications, the recall improvement may not justify the overhead.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Mul.what_goes_wrong: If query variants drift too far from the original intent (the LLM generates overly broad or tangential variants), the union of retrieved documents can become NOISY — including chunks relevant to the variant but not the user's actual question, diluting the context the final LLM sees. The larger candidate pool from multiple queries often needs a RERANKING step afterward to prioritize the most relevant chunks across all the retrieved candidates, adding another pipeline stage.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Mul.real_example: A user asks 'why was I charged twice?' — a multi-query retriever generates variants like 'duplicate billing charge', 'double payment error', and 'billing discrepancy refund process'; each retrieves somewhat different chunks from a support knowledge base (one might match a 'billing FAQ' page, another a 'refund process' page), and the union gives the final LLM access to BOTH relevant documents rather than just whichever one the original phrasing happened to match best.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Par.what_it_is: A LangChain retriever that indexes SMALL chunks ('children') for embedding/similarity search (for precise matching), but when a child chunk is retrieved, returns its LARGER 'parent' chunk or the full source document as the context passed to the LLM — combining precise retrieval with rich context.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Par.why_it_exists: There's a fundamental tension in chunk sizing: SMALL chunks embed/retrieve more precisely (a small chunk's embedding represents a focused idea, matching narrow queries well) but provide LESS CONTEXT to the LLM once retrieved (a small chunk alone may be ambiguous or missing surrounding explanation). ParentDocumentRetriever exists to get BOTH benefits — retrieve based on small, precise chunks, but generate using the larger context those chunks came from.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Par.how_it_works: During indexing, documents are split into LARGE 'parent' chunks, and each parent is further split into SMALL 'child' chunks. Only the CHILD chunks are embedded and stored in the vector store (for retrieval), but each child's metadata references its parent (stored separately, often in a simple document store / key-value store). At query time, similarity search finds the best-matching CHILD chunks, but the retriever then looks up and returns the corresponding PARENT chunks (deduplicated if multiple children share a parent) as the actual context passed to the LLM.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Par.use_when: Documents where small chunks retrieve well (precise semantic matching) but the LLM benefits from more surrounding context than a small chunk provides — e.g. technical documentation where a specific detail (small chunk) is best understood within its containing section (parent chunk).
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Par.avoid_when: If parent chunks are very large (e.g. entire long documents), retrieving the full parent for every match can quickly consume the context window if multiple distinct child matches map to different large parents — some size-capping on parents is usually still needed.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Par.what_goes_wrong: If multiple retrieved child chunks belong to the SAME parent, naive implementations might include that parent's content multiple times (redundancy) unless deduplication is handled. Choosing parent chunk size too large reintroduces the original problem (too much irrelevant context diluting the LLM's attention) — parent size still needs tuning, just at a different level than child size.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Par.real_example: A legal-document RAG system splits contracts into large 'section' parent chunks (~3000 chars) and small 'sentence-group' child chunks (~300 chars) for embedding; a query about a specific clause matches a precise child chunk, but the system returns the entire PARENT SECTION to the LLM — giving it the surrounding definitions and context needed to correctly interpret that specific clause, rather than just the isolated sentence.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.what_it_is: A LangChain retriever wrapper that takes the documents returned by a base retriever and COMPRESSES them — either by extracting only the relevant portions of each document (via an LLM or extraction model) or by filtering out entirely irrelevant documents — before passing the (smaller, more focused) result to the final LLM call.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.why_it_exists: Retrieved chunks, even when 'relevant' to the query overall, often contain a MIX of relevant and irrelevant text (a chunk might be mostly about topic X with one sentence about the query's actual topic Y) — passing the FULL chunk wastes context-window budget and can dilute the LLM's attention with irrelevant surrounding text. Contextual compression exists to extract just the parts of retrieved documents that are actually relevant to the SPECIFIC query, before final generation.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.how_it_works: Wraps a base retriever; after the base retriever returns documents, a 'compressor' processes each document — common compressors include: an LLM that extracts/rewrites only the query-relevant sentences from each document (`LLMChainExtractor`), a relevance-filter that DROPS documents below a relevance threshold entirely (`LLMChainFilter` or embedding-similarity-based filters), or a reranking model that reorders/filters by relevance score. The compressed/filtered set of documents is then returned as the retriever's output, used downstream as normal.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.use_when: Retrieved chunks tend to be large/multi-topic relative to specific queries, and reducing the context passed to the final LLM would improve both relevance/focus AND reduce token costs — particularly useful when chunk sizes are necessarily large (e.g. using ParentDocumentRetriever) but only small portions of each parent are relevant to a given query.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.avoid_when: Adds an extra LLM call (for LLM-based compressors) per retrieved document, increasing latency and cost — for small chunks that are already focused/relevant, or latency-sensitive applications, this overhead may not be worth it. Cheaper alternatives (embedding-similarity filtering rather than LLM extraction) can capture some benefit at lower cost.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.what_goes_wrong: LLM-based extraction compressors can be too AGGRESSIVE, stripping out context that seemed irrelevant in isolation but was actually needed for the final LLM to correctly interpret the remaining extracted text (e.g. removing a definition that a later sentence implicitly relies on). The extra LLM calls (one per retrieved document, potentially) can make this retrieval step the SLOWEST part of the pipeline if many documents are retrieved.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Con.real_example: A RAG system retrieves 3 large parent-document chunks (each ~2000 tokens, covering multiple subsections), but a `ContextualCompressionRetriever` with an LLM extractor reduces each to just the 1-2 sentences directly relevant to the user's specific question — shrinking the final prompt's context from ~6000 tokens to ~300 tokens while preserving the answer-relevant information, reducing both cost and irrelevant-context dilution.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ens.what_it_is: A LangChain retriever that COMBINES results from multiple underlying retrievers — typically a DENSE retriever (embedding-based similarity search, good at semantic/conceptual matches) and a SPARSE retriever (keyword-based, e.g. BM25, good at exact term/jargon matches) — merging and re-ranking their results (often via Reciprocal Rank Fusion) into a single result list.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ens.why_it_exists: Dense (embedding) retrieval excels at SEMANTIC similarity (synonyms, paraphrases, conceptual matches) but can underperform on queries involving exact keywords, codes, IDs, acronyms, or rare terms that weren't well-represented in the embedding model's training (e.g. a product SKU, an error code, a person's name). Sparse/keyword retrieval (BM25) excels at exact-term matching but misses semantic similarity (won't match 'automobile' to a document about 'cars'). Hybrid retrieval exists to get the COMPLEMENTARY STRENGTHS of both — catching both semantic and lexical matches.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ens.how_it_works: An `EnsembleRetriever` is configured with a list of retrievers (e.g. a vector-store-based dense retriever and a BM25 sparse retriever) and a weight for each. For a query, EACH retriever independently returns its top results; the `EnsembleRetriever` then combines these ranked lists using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) — a method that combines rankings from multiple sources by summing reciprocal-rank-based scores (`1/(rank + k)` for some constant k), giving documents that rank highly across MULTIPLE retrievers a higher combined score, without requiring the retrievers' raw scores to be on comparable scales.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ens.use_when: Corpora/queries where BOTH semantic similarity AND exact term matching matter — e.g. technical documentation with specific error codes/API names (sparse helps) alongside conceptual explanations (dense helps), or any domain where users sometimes search by exact terms and sometimes by description.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ens.avoid_when: For corpora/queries that are purely conceptual (no important exact-match terms, codes, or jargon), pure dense retrieval may perform just as well with less complexity — hybrid retrieval adds an extra retrieval pipeline (BM25 index maintenance alongside the vector store) and tuning (relative weights between dense and sparse) that may not be justified.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ens.what_goes_wrong: BM25 (sparse) indexes need to be MAINTAINED alongside the vector store — an extra piece of infrastructure that must stay in sync with the document corpus (added/removed documents need updating in both indexes). Tuning the relative WEIGHTS between dense and sparse retrievers in the ensemble is corpus/query-dependent and often requires evaluation (e.g. RAGAS) on representative queries to get right — a poorly-weighted ensemble can perform WORSE than either retriever alone if one retriever's noise dominates.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|RAG Pipelines|Ens.real_example: A code-documentation RAG system uses an `EnsembleRetriever` combining a dense retriever (matches conceptual queries like 'how do I handle errors') with a BM25 retriever (matches exact function/class names like 'HttpClientException') — a query mentioning a specific exception class name benefits from BM25's exact match, while a query asking 'how do I handle errors generally' benefits from the dense retriever's semantic understanding, and RRF combines both into a single relevant result set.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|HyDE.what_it_is: A retrieval technique where, instead of embedding the user's QUERY directly, an LLM first generates a HYPOTHETICAL ANSWER (a fabricated document that would plausibly answer the query) — and THAT hypothetical answer is embedded and used for similarity search against the actual document corpus.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|HyDE.why_it_exists: Questions and answers often have different LINGUISTIC STRUCTURE/vocabulary than the documents that contain the answer — a question ('What causes inflation?') may embed quite differently from a textbook passage explaining inflation's causes, even though they're semantically related. HyDE exists to bridge this query-document 'asymmetry' by generating something that LOOKS LIKE the target document (an answer-shaped passage) rather than something that looks like a question, improving the chance of embedding similarity to actual relevant documents.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|HyDE.how_it_works: Given a query, an LLM is prompted to generate a hypothetical passage that WOULD answer it (without access to the actual corpus — it's just using its parametric knowledge, and the generated passage may even be factually wrong). This hypothetical document is embedded (using the same embedding model as the corpus), and THIS embedding — not the original query's embedding — is used for similarity search against the vector store. The intuition is that the hypothetical answer's embedding is closer (in vector space) to ACTUAL relevant documents than the original question's embedding would be, because both the hypothetical and real documents share 'answer-like' structure/vocabulary.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|HyDE.use_when: Domains/queries where there's a significant STYLISTIC/STRUCTURAL gap between how questions are phrased and how answers/documents are written — e.g. short colloquial questions retrieving from formal technical documents.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|HyDE.avoid_when: Adds an extra LLM call (to generate the hypothetical document) per query, increasing latency/cost — for corpora where direct query embedding already retrieves well (e.g. FAQ-style documents that are themselves question-like), HyDE's benefit may not justify the overhead.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|HyDE.what_goes_wrong: The hypothetical document is GENERATED, not retrieved — if the LLM's generated 'hypothetical answer' is confidently WRONG or uses unusual phrasing/terminology not present in the actual corpus, its embedding may not actually be closer to relevant real documents, and retrieval quality can be WORSE than direct query embedding for some queries. This makes HyDE's benefit corpus- and query-dependent — it should be evaluated (e.g. with RAGAS) rather than assumed to always help.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|HyDE.real_example: A user asks a medical RAG system 'why do my knees hurt when it's cold?' — HyDE generates a hypothetical passage like 'Cold weather can cause joint pain due to changes in barometric pressure affecting synovial fluid viscosity and increased muscle tension around joints...' and embeds THIS passage; this 'answer-shaped' text is more likely to be close (in embedding space) to actual medical literature passages discussing cold-weather joint pain than the original casual question would be.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Mult.what_it_is: A retrieval technique where each document/chunk is represented by MULTIPLE different vectors — e.g. an embedding of a SUMMARY of the chunk, embeddings of HYPOTHETICAL QUESTIONS the chunk could answer, and/or an embedding of the raw chunk text itself — all pointing back to the same underlying chunk, increasing the chance that a user's query embedding will be close to AT LEAST ONE of these representations.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Mult.why_it_exists: A single embedding of the raw chunk text may not be the BEST representation for matching against user queries — users ask QUESTIONS, but chunks contain STATEMENTS/explanations; a chunk's SUMMARY might capture its gist more compactly (better for matching broad queries), while LLM-generated HYPOTHETICAL QUESTIONS that the chunk answers might match user queries more directly (similar motivation to HyDE, but generated at INDEXING time rather than query time). Multi-vector retrieval exists to give each piece of content several 'entry points' for retrieval.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Mult.how_it_works: During indexing, for each chunk, an LLM generates auxiliary representations (e.g. a 1-2 sentence summary, or 3-5 hypothetical questions the chunk would answer). EACH of these auxiliary texts is embedded SEPARATELY and stored in the vector index, with metadata pointing back to the ORIGINAL chunk. At query time, similarity search against ANY of these vectors (summary embeddings, question embeddings, or the raw chunk embedding) can retrieve the same underlying chunk — increasing recall by giving the chunk multiple 'representations' in embedding space that different query phrasings might match.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Mult.use_when: Corpora where chunks are dense/technical and users ask varied, sometimes tangential questions about their content — generating hypothetical questions/summaries at indexing time can pre-anticipate the diversity of ways users might ask about that content.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Mult.avoid_when: Significantly increases INDEXING cost (LLM calls per chunk to generate summaries/questions) and storage (multiple vectors per chunk) — for corpora where raw-chunk embedding already retrieves well, or where indexing cost/time is a major constraint (very large corpora), this overhead may not be justified.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Mult.what_goes_wrong: LLM-generated hypothetical questions/summaries can be GENERIC or fail to capture the chunk's most distinctive/important content — if the auxiliary representations don't meaningfully differ from (or improve upon) the raw chunk embedding, the extra indexing cost yields little retrieval benefit. Storage and retrieval-index size grow with the number of auxiliary vectors per chunk, which can affect vector-store performance/cost at scale.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Mult.real_example: For a technical API reference document, multi-vector retrieval generates hypothetical questions like 'How do I authenticate requests?' and 'What's the rate limit?' for the relevant chunks at indexing time; when a user later asks 'how many requests can I make per minute', this matches the pre-generated 'rate limit' question's embedding more directly than it would match the raw API-reference chunk's embedding (which is written in formal spec language, not question form).

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Self.what_it_is: A retriever that uses an LLM to PARSE a user's natural-language query into TWO parts: a semantic search component (the actual content to search for) AND structured METADATA FILTERS (extracted from phrases like 'from last year', 'by author Smith', 'in the engineering department') — then performs filtered similarity search using both.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Self.why_it_exists: Users often express FILTERING INTENT in natural language mixed with their semantic query ('show me reviews from 2023 about battery life') — but vector similarity search alone treats the entire query as one semantic blob, potentially missing that 'from 2023' should be a METADATA FILTER rather than something to semantically match against. Self-query retrieval exists to automatically DECOMPOSE such queries into the right combination of semantic search + structured filters, without requiring users to use a separate filter UI or structured query syntax.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Self.how_it_works: The retriever is configured with a description of the metadata SCHEMA available for filtering (e.g. 'documents have a `year` (int), `author` (string), `department` (string) metadata fields'). Given a user query, an LLM is prompted (using this schema description) to output a structured representation: a semantic search string PLUS a filter expression (e.g. `year == 2023`). The retriever then executes the underlying vector store's filtered search using both — embedding the semantic portion for similarity search, and applying the extracted filter as a metadata constraint.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Self.use_when: Corpora with rich, queryable metadata (dates, categories, authors, departments, ratings) where users naturally express filtering criteria in conversational language rather than using a separate structured filter UI.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Self.avoid_when: Corpora with no meaningful metadata to filter on, or where users always use a separate explicit filter UI (so filter extraction from natural language isn't needed) — the LLM-based query parsing adds latency/cost and a potential failure point for no benefit in that case.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Self.what_goes_wrong: The LLM can MISPARSE the query — e.g. extracting an incorrect filter value, applying a filter the user didn't intend (over-constraining results to zero), or failing to recognize a filter-like phrase as a filter (treating 'recent' as semantic content rather than a date filter, which it also can't directly translate to a precise date range without ambiguity). Schema descriptions need to be kept in sync with the ACTUAL metadata present in the vector store — if the LLM is told about a `department` field that's inconsistently populated across documents, filters on it may exclude relevant documents that lack that field.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Self.real_example: A user queries a product-review RAG system: 'what do people say about the camera on phones released after 2022?' — a self-query retriever extracts the semantic component 'opinions about camera quality' and a metadata filter `release_year > 2022`, then performs similarity search for camera-related content ONLY among reviews of phones meeting that filter — something pure similarity search couldn't reliably do, since 'after 2022' isn't a semantic concept embeddings naturally capture precisely.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Rera.what_it_is: A two-stage retrieval pattern: an initial (fast but less precise) retrieval step — e.g. embedding-based similarity search — returns a larger candidate set (e.g. top-50), and a SECOND model, a CROSS-ENCODER (which jointly processes the query AND each candidate document together, rather than embedding them separately), RE-SCORES and re-orders these candidates to produce a smaller, more precisely-ranked final set (e.g. top-5) passed to the LLM.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Rera.why_it_exists: Embedding-based (bi-encoder) retrieval embeds the query and documents INDEPENDENTLY and compares via vector similarity — fast and scalable (can search millions of documents), but the independence means the model never directly 'looks at' the query and document together, limiting how precisely it can judge relevance. Cross-encoders, which process (query, document) pairs JOINTLY through a transformer, can capture much finer-grained relevance signals — but are too SLOW to run against an entire corpus for every query. Reranking exists to get cross-encoder precision where it matters (the final ranking of a small candidate set) while keeping the initial broad search fast (bi-encoder/ANN).
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Rera.how_it_works: Stage 1 (retrieval): embedding-based similarity search (or hybrid dense+sparse) retrieves a relatively large candidate set (e.g. top-20 to top-100) — optimizing for RECALL (don't miss relevant documents) over precision. Stage 2 (reranking): a cross-encoder model (e.g. a fine-tuned BERT-style model, or API-based rerankers like Cohere Rerank) takes the (query, candidate) pair for EACH candidate and outputs a relevance score by jointly attending over both texts — these scores are used to RE-SORT the candidates, and only the TOP-FEW (e.g. top-3 to top-5) after reranking are passed to the final LLM as context.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Rera.use_when: Production RAG systems where retrieval recall is reasonable (relevant documents ARE in the top-20/50) but PRECISION at the top needs improvement (the most relevant document isn't always ranked #1 by embedding similarity alone) — reranking is one of the highest-ROI additions to a RAG pipeline for improving the relevance of what the LLM actually sees.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Rera.avoid_when: Adds latency (an additional model call processing multiple candidates) — for latency-critical applications where the initial retrieval is already sufficiently precise (e.g. very narrow, well-curated corpora), reranking's marginal benefit may not justify the added latency.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Rera.what_goes_wrong: If the INITIAL retrieval (stage 1) doesn't include the truly relevant document in its candidate set at all (a recall failure), reranking can't fix it — reranking can only RE-ORDER what's already retrieved, so a too-small initial candidate set (e.g. top-5 instead of top-50) can bottleneck overall quality regardless of reranker quality. Cross-encoder reranking cost scales with the NUMBER OF CANDIDATES — reranking a very large candidate set (e.g. top-200) can become a latency bottleneck itself.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Rera.real_example: A RAG pipeline retrieves the top-25 chunks via embedding similarity (optimizing for recall — catching anything plausibly relevant), then a Cohere Rerank API call re-scores all 25 against the query and returns the top-4 by cross-encoder relevance — these 4, often a DIFFERENT and more precisely relevant set than simply taking the top-4 by raw embedding similarity, are passed to the LLM for generation.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Grap.what_it_is: A RAG approach that combines a KNOWLEDGE GRAPH (entities and their relationships, extracted from documents) with vector-based retrieval — allowing queries to be answered using both semantic similarity search AND graph traversal/structured relationship queries (e.g. 'find all companies connected to Person X through board memberships').
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Grap.why_it_exists: Pure vector-based RAG struggles with queries that require MULTI-HOP REASONING over relationships between entities (e.g. 'which suppliers of Company A are also customers of Company B?') — no single chunk likely contains this combined information, and similarity search retrieves chunks based on TEXT similarity, not relational structure. GraphRAG exists to capture and query the RELATIONAL/STRUCTURAL knowledge implicit in documents (who is connected to whom, what depends on what), enabling reasoning that traverses these relationships explicitly, which pure text-chunk retrieval cannot do.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Grap.how_it_works: During indexing, an LLM extracts ENTITIES (people, organizations, concepts) and RELATIONSHIPS between them from source documents, constructing a knowledge graph (often stored in a graph database like Neo4j). Some GraphRAG implementations (e.g. Microsoft's GraphRAG) additionally cluster the graph into COMMUNITIES of related entities and generate SUMMARIES of each community (useful for high-level/global questions about the corpus, like 'what are the main themes across all documents?', which pure chunk-retrieval handles poorly since no single chunk summarizes the whole corpus). At query time, depending on the query type, the system may: traverse the graph to follow relationships (multi-hop queries), retrieve community summaries (global/thematic queries), or fall back to standard vector similarity search over text chunks (local/specific queries) — sometimes combining multiple of these.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Grap.use_when: Corpora rich in INTERCONNECTED ENTITIES where queries often require understanding RELATIONSHIPS (organizational charts, supply chains, research citation networks, character relationships in narratives) or GLOBAL/THEMATIC questions about the whole corpus that no single chunk answers.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Grap.avoid_when: Significant additional complexity/cost — building and maintaining a knowledge graph (entity/relationship extraction via LLM is expensive at scale, and the graph needs updating as documents change) is substantial overhead compared to standard chunk-based RAG. For corpora/queries that are well-served by retrieving relevant TEXT PASSAGES (most FAQ/document-search use cases), standard RAG is far simpler and likely sufficient.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Grap.what_goes_wrong: Entity/relationship EXTRACTION via LLM is imperfect — entities can be inconsistently named/deduplicated across documents (e.g. 'IBM' vs 'International Business Machines' treated as different entities unless resolved), and extracted relationships can be incomplete or incorrect, propagating errors into the graph that affect all queries traversing through them. The extraction/indexing cost (LLM calls per document to extract entities/relationships, plus community detection/summarization) is substantially higher than standard chunking+embedding, making GraphRAG a heavier investment that needs to be justified by query patterns that actually benefit from graph structure.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Grap.real_example: A GraphRAG system over a corpus of corporate filings extracts entities (companies, executives, board members) and relationships (e.g. 'serves on board of', 'subsidiary of'); a query like 'what other companies share a board member with Company X?' is answered by traversing the graph from Company X's board members to OTHER companies they serve on the boards of — information that's spread across many different filing documents and would be essentially impossible to answer via chunk-similarity retrieval alone.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Agen.what_it_is: A RAG pattern where retrieval is not a FIXED step in every query's pipeline, but a TOOL that an LLM AGENT decides whether and when to invoke — the agent can choose to retrieve (possibly multiple times, with different queries, from different sources), reason about retrieved results, retrieve AGAIN if results are insufficient, or skip retrieval entirely if it judges the query doesn't need it.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Agen.why_it_exists: Standard RAG always retrieves-then-generates, even for queries that don't need external information (e.g. 'what's 2+2?' or 'summarize the text I just gave you') — wasting a retrieval call and potentially injecting IRRELEVANT context that confuses the model. Conversely, some complex queries need MULTIPLE retrieval steps (retrieve, realize the first results are insufficient, reformulate, retrieve again) — a single fixed retrieval step can't adapt. Agentic RAG exists to make retrieval a DYNAMIC, AGENT-CONTROLLED decision — retrieve when needed, as many times as needed, from whichever source is appropriate, rather than as a rigid one-shot pipeline stage.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Agen.how_it_works: The retriever (possibly multiple retrievers over different corpora/sources) is exposed to the LLM as a TOOL (with a description of what it searches and when to use it), within an agent loop (e.g. ReAct-style: the agent reasons about what it needs, calls the retrieval tool if appropriate, observes results, and either answers or retrieves again with a refined query). The agent might also have OTHER tools available (calculators, APIs, other retrievers) and decides among them based on the query — retrieval becomes one option among several, chosen contextually rather than always executed.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Agen.use_when: Applications where queries vary widely in whether/how much external knowledge they require, where MULTIPLE distinct knowledge sources exist (and the agent should pick the right one(s) per query), or where complex queries benefit from iterative retrieval (retrieve, evaluate sufficiency, retrieve more if needed).
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Agen.avoid_when: For applications where EVERY query genuinely needs retrieval from a SINGLE known source (e.g. a documentation-only Q&A bot where every question is about the docs), a fixed RAG pipeline is simpler, faster (no agent reasoning overhead), and more predictable than giving an agent the 'choice' to retrieve.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Agen.what_goes_wrong: Agent reasoning about WHETHER to retrieve adds latency and cost (extra LLM calls for the reasoning/decision steps) compared to always-retrieve pipelines — and the agent can make WRONG decisions (skipping retrieval when it shouldn't, or retrieving unnecessarily, or retrieving with poorly-formulated queries). Multi-step agentic retrieval loops can also loop excessively (repeatedly retrieving without converging) without proper iteration limits/guardrails.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Agen.real_example: A general-purpose assistant has access to both a company-document retriever AND a web-search tool, plus a calculator; for 'what's our Q3 revenue compared to industry average', the agent might first retrieve the company's Q3 revenue from internal documents, then use web search to find industry-average figures, then use the calculator to compute the comparison — three different tool calls chosen dynamically based on what information is needed at each step, something a single fixed retrieval pipeline couldn't orchestrate.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|RAGA.what_it_is: RAGAS (RAG Assessment) is an evaluation FRAMEWORK providing metrics specifically for RAG pipelines, including FAITHFULNESS (does the generated answer's claims actually follow from/are supported by the retrieved context, i.e. is it free of hallucination relative to the context?), ANSWER RELEVANCY (does the answer actually address the user's question?), and CONTEXT RECALL (did retrieval find ALL the information needed to answer the question, measured against a ground-truth reference)?
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|RAGA.why_it_exists: RAG pipelines have MULTIPLE potential failure points (bad retrieval, bad generation given good retrieval, good retrieval but irrelevant generation) — a single end-to-end 'is the answer correct' metric doesn't tell you WHICH component failed. RAGAS exists to provide COMPONENT-LEVEL metrics that isolate retrieval quality from generation quality, enabling targeted debugging/improvement (e.g. 'context recall is low → fix retrieval/chunking' vs 'faithfulness is low → fix the generation prompt/model').
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|RAGA.how_it_works: Most RAGAS metrics use an LLM-AS-JUDGE approach: FAITHFULNESS is computed by decomposing the generated answer into individual claims/statements, then checking (via LLM) whether each claim is supported by the retrieved context — the faithfulness score is the fraction of claims that ARE supported (catches hallucination — the answer saying things NOT in the retrieved context). ANSWER RELEVANCY is computed by having an LLM generate questions that the GIVEN ANSWER would answer, then measuring how similar those generated questions are to the ORIGINAL question (an answer that's relevant should make the LLM 'reverse-engineer' something close to the original question). CONTEXT RECALL compares the retrieved context against a ground-truth/reference answer (often requiring labeled data) — measuring whether the information needed for the reference answer IS PRESENT in the retrieved context.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|RAGA.use_when: Systematically evaluating and comparing RAG pipeline configurations (different chunking strategies, embedding models, retrieval methods, prompts) on a representative set of queries — essential for any RAG system beyond a quick prototype, to know whether changes actually improve quality and WHERE in the pipeline problems lie.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|RAGA.avoid_when: RAGAS's LLM-as-judge metrics have a cost (LLM calls per evaluation) and inherit LLM-as-judge limitations (consistency, potential biases) — for very early prototyping, simpler spot-checking by humans on a handful of examples may suffice before investing in a full RAGAS evaluation pipeline.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|RAGA.what_goes_wrong: Context recall requires GROUND-TRUTH reference answers/contexts — creating a labeled evaluation dataset is itself significant work, and without it, context recall can't be measured (though faithfulness and answer relevancy don't strictly require ground truth). LLM-as-judge metrics can be NOISY/inconsistent run-to-run, and absolute metric VALUES are less meaningful than RELATIVE comparisons between configurations evaluated under identical conditions — teams should use RAGAS scores to compare A/B configurations, not as absolute quality certifications.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|RAGA.real_example: A team evaluates two chunking strategies (fixed 500-char vs recursive 1000-char with overlap) on the same 50-query evaluation set using RAGAS: if recursive chunking shows higher context recall (retrieval finds the needed info more often) AND higher faithfulness (generated answers stick to retrieved context better, likely because chunks are more coherent), this gives concrete evidence to adopt the recursive strategy — rather than relying on a few spot-checked examples.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Cont.what_it_is: Two retrieval-focused RAGAS metrics: CONTEXT PRECISION measures whether the retrieved chunks that ARE relevant are ranked HIGHER than irrelevant ones (i.e. is the relevant information near the top of the retrieved set, where the LLM is more likely to attend to it?), while CONTEXT RECALL measures whether ALL the information needed to answer the question (per a ground-truth reference) was retrieved AT ALL, regardless of ranking.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Cont.why_it_exists: Retrieval can fail in two distinct ways: (1) relevant information simply isn't retrieved at all (a RECALL failure — no amount of reranking or prompting can fix this, since the LLM never sees it), or (2) relevant information IS retrieved but BURIED among irrelevant chunks (a PRECISION failure — the LLM has access to what it needs but may not weight it appropriately amid noise). These two metrics exist to DISTINGUISH these failure modes, since the fixes differ — recall failures point to chunking/embedding/retrieval-method issues (need a fundamentally different/larger retrieval), while precision failures point to RERANKING or retrieval count (k) issues.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Cont.how_it_works: Context recall: given a ground-truth reference answer (or reference context), an LLM judge checks whether each piece of information in the reference IS PRESENT somewhere in the retrieved chunks — the score is the fraction of reference information that's covered by retrieval. Context precision: for each retrieved chunk, an LLM judge determines whether it's RELEVANT to the question; the precision score rewards configurations where relevant chunks appear EARLIER in the ranked retrieval results (using a precision@k-style calculation across ranks) — a retrieval that returns 1 relevant chunk first and 9 irrelevant ones scores higher than one that returns the same 1 relevant chunk last.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Cont.use_when: Diagnosing WHY a RAG pipeline underperforms — running both metrics on a failing query set tells you whether to focus engineering effort on RETRIEVAL COVERAGE (recall — try different embedding models, hybrid retrieval, query expansion) or RETRIEVAL RANKING (precision — add/improve reranking, reduce noise in chunking).
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Cont.avoid_when: Both require either ground-truth references (context recall) or per-chunk relevance judgments (context precision, via LLM) — for rapid early iteration without labeled data, these metrics aren't computable; simpler proxy signals (e.g. whether the final answer is correct, judged by a human) may need to suffice initially.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Cont.what_goes_wrong: Low context recall is often MISDIAGNOSED as a generation/prompting problem (since the symptom — wrong/incomplete answers — looks the same from outside) when the actual fix needed is in retrieval (different chunking, different embedding model, hybrid search) — teams that only look at end-to-end answer quality without context-recall measurement can spend significant effort tuning prompts that can never fix an underlying recall problem.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|Cont.real_example: A RAG system gives incomplete answers to multi-part questions; measuring context recall reveals that for ~30% of such questions, only ONE of the two needed facts is present in the retrieved chunks — pointing to a RETRIEVAL gap (perhaps chunk size is too small, splitting related facts into separate chunks that don't both get retrieved) rather than a generation/prompting issue, redirecting engineering effort appropriately.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|TruL.what_it_is: Open-source frameworks (alongside RAGAS) for evaluating LLM applications — TruLens focuses on instrumenting and tracking 'feedback functions' (custom or built-in evaluation metrics) over LLM app traces with a dashboard for inspection; DeepEval provides a pytest-like testing framework for LLM outputs with built-in metrics (hallucination, relevancy, bias, toxicity, RAG-specific metrics) designed to integrate into CI/CD pipelines.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|TruL.why_it_exists: Different teams need different evaluation WORKFLOWS — some want deep observability/debugging tooling integrated with tracing (TruLens's niche, often paired with its 'RAG triad' of metrics: context relevance, groundedness, answer relevance), others want LLM evaluation to feel like UNIT TESTING that can run in CI/CD and fail a build (DeepEval's `assert` -based, pytest-integrated approach). These frameworks exist to provide opinionated, ready-made tooling for these different evaluation workflows, rather than every team building custom evaluation harnesses from scratch.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|TruL.how_it_works: TruLens: wraps/instruments an LLM application (chains, agents) to capture traces, and applies 'feedback functions' (Python functions, often LLM-based, that score some aspect of a trace — e.g. groundedness of the response in retrieved context) to each trace; results are viewable in a dashboard for comparing different app versions/configurations. DeepEval: provides metric classes (e.g. `HallucinationMetric`, `AnswerRelevancyMetric`, `ContextualPrecisionMetric`) that can be used in pytest-style test functions — `assert_test(test_case, [metric1, metric2])` — so LLM evaluation runs alongside regular software tests, with pass/fail thresholds, and can gate CI/CD pipelines.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|TruL.use_when: TruLens for deep observability/debugging during development, especially comparing multiple RAG configurations side-by-side in a dashboard. DeepEval when the team wants LLM quality checks to be part of the standard TEST SUITE / CI pipeline, with pass/fail semantics like traditional unit tests.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|TruL.avoid_when: For teams already invested in RAGAS + LangSmith (a common combination), introducing an additional evaluation framework adds tooling overhead — these frameworks have overlapping capabilities, and most teams pick ONE primary evaluation stack rather than running several in parallel.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|TruL.what_goes_wrong: Like all LLM-as-judge-based evaluation, metrics from these frameworks are subject to judge-model bias/inconsistency — treating a DeepEval `assert_test` failure as a hard 'bug' (like a traditional unit test failure) can be misleading if the underlying metric is noisy; teams need calibration (e.g. checking that the LLM judge's verdicts correlate with human judgment on a sample) before trusting these as CI GATES that block deploys.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|TruL.real_example: A team adds DeepEval tests to their CI pipeline: for a set of regression test cases (query + expected-topic), a `HallucinationMetric` and `AnswerRelevancyMetric` run against the RAG pipeline's output on every pull request — if a prompt change causes faithfulness to drop below a threshold on these regression cases, the CI build fails, catching a regression before it reaches production, similar to how a failing unit test would block a code change.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|A/B.what_it_is: The practice of running TWO (or more) different RAG pipeline configurations (different chunking strategies, embedding models, retrieval methods, prompts, or LLMs) in PARALLEL — either offline against an evaluation dataset, or online against live user traffic — and comparing their performance using metrics (RAGAS scores, user satisfaction, task completion rates) to decide which configuration to adopt.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|A/B.why_it_exists: RAG pipeline design involves many INTERACTING choices (chunk size, embedding model, retrieval method, reranking, prompt wording) whose effects on end quality are often NOT predictable from first principles or single-example testing — A/B testing exists to make these decisions EMPIRICALLY, based on measured outcomes on representative queries/users, rather than intuition, especially since a change that improves one type of query might degrade another.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|A/B.how_it_works: OFFLINE A/B testing: run both configurations against the SAME evaluation dataset (a fixed set of queries, ideally with ground-truth references for metrics like context recall), compute RAGAS/other metrics for each configuration, and compare. ONLINE A/B testing: route a percentage of LIVE user traffic to configuration A and the rest to configuration B (randomized), and compare downstream metrics — user satisfaction ratings, follow-up question rates (a proxy for 'the first answer wasn't sufficient'), task completion, or explicit feedback (thumbs up/down) — over a sufficient sample size to reach statistical significance.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|A/B.use_when: Before rolling out a significant RAG pipeline change (new embedding model, new chunking strategy, new prompt) to ALL users — especially in production systems where a regression could affect many users, A/B testing (at least offline, ideally also a limited online rollout) de-risks the change.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|A/B.avoid_when: For very early-stage prototypes with no real user traffic and limited evaluation data, formal A/B testing infrastructure is premature — simpler before/after comparisons on a small evaluation set suffice until the system has enough usage/data for statistically meaningful online tests.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|A/B.what_goes_wrong: Online A/B tests need SUFFICIENT SAMPLE SIZE and DURATION to reach statistical significance — concluding 'B is better' from a small number of interactions risks acting on noise. Offline evaluation-dataset results don't always predict ONLINE outcomes — an evaluation set built early in a project can become STALE relative to actual user query patterns, so periodic refresh of evaluation datasets (incorporating real anonymized user queries, where privacy permits) is important for A/B results to remain meaningful.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|Advanced RAG|A/B.real_example: A team A/B tests adding a reranking step to their RAG pipeline: offline, RAGAS context precision improves significantly with reranking on their evaluation set; they then roll out reranking to 10% of live traffic and monitor user 'thumbs down' rates over two weeks — confirming the offline improvement translates to fewer negative feedback signals before rolling out to 100% of users, since reranking also adds latency that could itself negatively affect user experience in ways the offline metric doesn't capture.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.what_it_is: A legacy LangChain chain that converts a natural-language question into a SQL query (via an LLM, given the database schema), executes that query against a connected database, and returns the result — optionally also using the result to generate a natural-language answer.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.why_it_exists: Business users/analysts often know WHAT they want to know ('how many orders did we ship last month?') but don't know SQL — `SQLDatabaseChain` exists to let an LLM bridge natural language and SQL, giving non-technical users a conversational interface to structured databases without writing queries themselves.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.how_it_works: The chain is given a database connection; it introspects the schema (table names, columns, types — sometimes sample rows) and includes this schema description in a prompt along with the user's natural-language question, asking the LLM to generate a SQL query. The chain then EXECUTES this generated SQL against the database (using the connection) and returns the raw result (and/or feeds the result back to the LLM to produce a natural-language summary of the answer).
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.use_when: Prototyping natural-language interfaces over structured databases — e.g. an internal tool ('InventoryBot') where staff ask questions like 'how many units of SKU-123 are in the Chicago warehouse?' and get answers without writing SQL themselves.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.avoid_when: In production with WRITE access to databases or sensitive data — letting an LLM generate and EXECUTE arbitrary SQL against a real database is a significant security/safety risk (see what_goes_wrong). Also largely superseded in current LangChain by LCEL-based alternatives (`create_sql_query_chain` + a separate execution tool) that offer more control over the generate-vs-execute boundary.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.what_goes_wrong: SQL INJECTION-STYLE RISK: if the LLM generates a destructive query (`DROP TABLE`, `DELETE FROM ... WHERE 1=1`, or a query that exposes data the user shouldn't see) and the chain blindly executes it, real damage/data-leakage can occur — production systems MUST restrict the database connection to a READ-ONLY user/role with access only to specific tables/views, and ideally validate/sandbox generated SQL before execution. The LLM can also generate SYNTACTICALLY INVALID or semantically WRONG SQL (e.g. misunderstanding column meanings, joining tables incorrectly) — producing a confidently-wrong answer that LOOKS correct because it ran without error.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.real_example: An 'InventoryBot' connects to a read-only replica of the inventory database with a DB user that only has SELECT privileges on `products`, `inventory`, and `warehouses` tables; a staff member asks 'which products are below reorder threshold in the East region warehouses?' and the chain generates and executes a `SELECT ... JOIN ... WHERE quantity < reorder_threshold AND region = 'East'` query — the read-only restriction means even if the LLM hallucinated a `DELETE` statement, the database would reject it, limiting the blast radius of a bad generation.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.what_it_is: An LCEL-based LangChain function/chain that generates a SQL query from a natural-language question and database schema — but, unlike `SQLDatabaseChain`, does NOT itself execute the query, returning just the generated SQL string for the calling code to handle (validate, execute, log, etc.) separately.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.why_it_exists: `SQLDatabaseChain`'s bundling of GENERATION and EXECUTION into one opaque step makes it hard to insert safety checks (query validation, dry-run/EXPLAIN, human review) between the two — `create_sql_query_chain` exists to SEPARATE these concerns: generate the SQL as one explicit, inspectable LCEL step, then let the application decide how/whether to execute it, composing with other LCEL pieces (like `QuerySQLDataBaseTool`) as needed.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.how_it_works: Given a database connection (for schema introspection) and an LLM, `create_sql_query_chain(llm, db)` returns a Runnable that, when invoked with `{'question': '...'}`, produces a SQL query string — using the schema (and optionally sample rows) in its prompt, similar to `SQLDatabaseChain`'s generation step, but stopping there. This Runnable can then be CHAINED (via `|`) with a separate execution step (e.g. `QuerySQLDataBaseTool`) explicitly, with whatever validation/logging/guardrails the application wants in between.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.use_when: Building NL-to-SQL applications where you want explicit control over the generate→validate→execute pipeline — e.g. logging generated queries for audit, running them through a SQL linter/validator, or requiring human approval before execution for certain query types.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.avoid_when: For the simplest possible prototypes where bundling generation+execution (`SQLDatabaseChain`) is 'good enough' and the separation of concerns isn't yet needed — though even prototypes benefit from at least READ-ONLY database permissions regardless of which chain abstraction is used.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.what_goes_wrong: Because this chain only GENERATES SQL, it's easy to forget that the generated SQL still needs to be validated/sandboxed before execution — the separation of concerns is only a SAFETY BENEFIT if the application actually USES it to add validation; simply piping the output directly to execution with no checks provides no more safety than `SQLDatabaseChain`.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.real_example: `write_query = create_sql_query_chain(llm, db)` generates SQL from a question; before executing, the application runs the generated SQL through `EXPLAIN` to verify it's a `SELECT`-only query touching only allowed tables, logs it for audit, and ONLY THEN passes it to `QuerySQLDataBaseTool` for execution — a workflow that `SQLDatabaseChain`'s single opaque step doesn't naturally support.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.what_it_is: A LangChain tool that EXECUTES a given SQL query string against a connected database and returns the results (as a string representation of rows) — designed to be used as the execution half of an NL-to-SQL pipeline (often paired with `create_sql_query_chain` for generation), or as a tool available to an agent.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.why_it_exists: Separating SQL EXECUTION into its own tool exists for the same reason as `create_sql_query_chain` separating generation — composability and safety. As a TOOL, it can also be given directly to an AGENT (alongside other tools), letting the agent decide when/whether to query the database as part of a broader reasoning loop, rather than being a fixed pipeline step.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.how_it_works: Configured with a database connection, `QuerySQLDataBaseTool.run(sql_query_string)` executes the given SQL against the database and returns the result rows formatted as a string (suitable for inclusion in an LLM's context/observation in an agent loop). As a Runnable, it can be chained (`generate_query | QuerySQLDataBaseTool`) for a pipeline, or registered as a tool for an agent that decides when to call it.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.use_when: Building the execution step of an NL-to-SQL pipeline where you want it as a discrete, swappable/inspectable component — e.g. to add logging, error handling, or result post-processing (formatting, truncation for very large result sets) between query generation and final answer generation.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.avoid_when: Without restricting the underlying DATABASE CONNECTION's permissions (read-only, limited tables), using this tool to execute LLM-GENERATED SQL carries the same risks as `SQLDatabaseChain` — the tool itself does not add safety, it's purely an execution mechanism; safety must come from connection-level permissions and/or query validation upstream.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.what_goes_wrong: Result sets can be very LARGE (a generated query might inadvertently `SELECT *` from a huge table) — returning the full result as a string can blow up the LLM's context window in the next step; production usage typically needs result truncation/pagination/summarization before feeding results back to an LLM. Errors from invalid SQL (the generation step produced something that doesn't match the actual schema) surface as raw database error messages — these can be returned to the agent as an 'observation' for it to retry/fix, but need handling so a malformed query doesn't crash the whole pipeline.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.real_example: In a ReAct-style agent with database access, the agent generates a SQL query, calls `QuerySQLDataBaseTool` to execute it, and gets back either results or an error message (e.g. 'column "custmer_id" does not exist') as its 'observation' — the agent can then NOTICE the typo-like error and retry with a corrected query (`customer_id`), demonstrating the iterative generate-execute-observe-retry loop that pure `SQLDatabaseChain` doesn't support.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.what_it_is: LangChain's `SQLDatabase` utility class (built on SQLAlchemy) provides a unified interface for connecting to various relational databases — PostgreSQL, SQLite, SQL Server, MySQL, etc. — via SQLAlchemy connection strings, enabling schema introspection and query execution regardless of the underlying database engine.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.why_it_exists: NL-to-SQL chains need to work with WHATEVER database the application uses — building database-specific connection/introspection logic for every supported engine would be redundant. By building on SQLAlchemy (which already abstracts over many database dialects), LangChain's `SQLDatabase` class gets broad database support 'for free', with the main per-database work being installing the right SQLAlchemy DRIVER (`psycopg2` for Postgres, `pyodbc`/`pymssql` for SQL Server, built-in `sqlite3` for SQLite) and constructing the correct connection string.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.how_it_works: `SQLDatabase.from_uri('postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/dbname')` (or the equivalent SQLite/SQL Server connection string) creates a `SQLDatabase` instance that can: introspect the schema (`get_table_info()` returns DDL/column info for use in prompts), execute queries (`run(sql)`), and optionally restrict which tables are visible to the LLM (`include_tables=[...]`) — limiting both the prompt size (schema description) and the SCOPE of what an LLM-generated query could touch.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.use_when: Any NL-to-SQL application — the choice of database engine (Postgres for production apps, SQLite for local prototypes/demos, SQL Server for enterprise environments) doesn't change the LangChain-side code beyond the connection string and driver installation.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.avoid_when: N/A as a general utility — but the CONNECTION CREDENTIALS used should always be a restricted (read-only, limited-table) database user/role for any LLM-facing connection, regardless of which database engine.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.what_goes_wrong: Missing database DRIVERS (e.g. `psycopg2` not installed for Postgres) produce import/connection errors that can be confusing if the error doesn't clearly indicate 'driver not installed' vs 'connection failed'. Connection strings containing CREDENTIALS are easy to accidentally hardcode/commit to source control — these should come from environment variables/secrets management, especially since (as discussed elsewhere) credentials committed to git history persist even after later removal.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.real_example: A prototype uses `SQLDatabase.from_uri('sqlite:///inventory.db')` for local development with a sample SQLite file, then switches to `SQLDatabase.from_uri(os.environ['DATABASE_URL'])` (a Postgres connection string from an environment variable, pointing to a read-only replica) for production — the LangChain-side NL-to-SQL chain code is UNCHANGED, only the connection configuration differs.

5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.what_it_is: A capability of modern LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) where the model can be given a list of available 'tools'/'functions', each described by a JSON SCHEMA (name, description, parameter types/structure) — and the model can respond by requesting to CALL one of these functions with specific arguments (formatted according to the schema) instead of (or in addition to) generating plain text.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.why_it_exists: LLMs need a RELIABLE way to interact with external systems (APIs, databases, code execution) and to produce STRUCTURED output that downstream code can parse without ambiguity. Function/tool calling exists to let model providers TRAIN models specifically to recognize when a function call is appropriate and to produce well-formed, schema-conforming arguments — far more reliable than asking the model to 'output JSON in this format' via plain prompting alone, since the model has been fine-tuned/constrained specifically for this output mode.
5|🔴 T1 RAG & LangChain|SQL & Tool Chains.how_it_works: The application defines a list of tools, each with a `name`, `description` (telling the model WHEN/WHY to use it), and a JSON Schema for its parameters (types, required fields, enums, etc.). This list is sent alongside the conversation to the LLM API. The model's response can include a `tool_calls` field — specifying which tool(s) to call and with what arguments (as JSON matching the schema) — instead of (or alongside) a text response. The APPLICATION then executes the actual function/tool (the model doesn't execute anything itself), and the result is sent back to the model (as a 'tool' role message) for it to incorporate into a final response — this is the core mechanism underlying AGENTS.
